topics: Secondary Plans, planning;
brief: Staff update council on the Our Scarborough Centre secondary plan study, which will guide growth around the future subway extension. Council is asked to direct staff to bring the amendments to a public meeting in fall 2025. No zoning change is decided in this item.

title: Kingston Road, between Midland Avenue and Brimley Road/Brimley Road South - Speed Limit Review
topics: speed limits, traffic; motor vehicle traffic; motorized traffic; traffic conditions; traffic flow; trip info; tripinfo
brief: Staff recommend lowering the speed limit from 60 km/h to 50 km/h on Kingston Road between Midland Avenue and Brimley Road, matching the limit on Kingston Road west of Midland Avenue. Because the TTC runs buses there, city council approval is required.

title: 4610 Finch Avenue East - Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: [buildings by height], long term care homes, rezoning; homes for the aged; long term care centers; long term care centres; long term care facilities; nursing facilities; nursing homes, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: City staff recommend approving zoning changes to allow a 13-storey building at 4610 Finch Avenue East with a 378-bed long-term care home, an ambulance depot and medical offices, on a city-owned site. The building would total 40,020 square metres. Council would amend the zoning by-law to permit the project.

title: Review of the Order Paper
brief: This is a procedural item: City Council reviews the order paper, the list of items to be considered at the meeting. No decision is being asked for.

title: Presentations, Introductions and Announcements
brief: This is a procedural item: the City Council meeting includes various presentations, introductions and announcements. No decisions are being asked for at this stage.

title: Petitions
brief: This is a procedural item: members of council may file petitions during the meeting for the record. No decision is being asked for at this stage.

title: Declarations of Interest
brief: This is a procedural item: councillors declare any interests they hold under the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act. No decision is being asked for at this stage.

title: Introduction of Committee Reports, New Business and Business Previously Requested from the Mayor and City Officials
brief: This is a procedural item: the mayor and committee chairs introduce committee reports, new business and business previously requested from the mayor and city officials — including reports from the Executive, Audit, Board of Health, Civic Appointments, Economic and Community Development, General Government, Infrastructure and Environment, and Planning and Housing committees and the four community councils. No decision is being asked for.

title: Confirmation of Minutes
brief: This is a procedural item: City Council will confirm the minutes from its regular meeting held on June 25 and 26, 2025, as an accurate record.

title: Call to Order
brief: This is a procedural item: the City Council meeting opens with the call to order, O Canada and a moment of silence. No decision is being asked for.

title: Amendments to Municipal Code Chapter 103: Heritage
topics: change, heritage designation, municipal codes; amendments; conversion; modification
brief: The city's heritage by-law would be updated to match recent provincial changes to the Ontario Heritage Act, and the Chief Planner would get authority to handle routine heritage decisions such as easement agreements. Council decides on the technical amendments to Municipal Code Chapter 103. Staff would also run a full review of the chapter and report back on modernizing it.

title: Missing Middle and Midrise Housing Implementation Initiative
topics: housing, ownership housing; homes; residences
brief: Council is being asked to direct city planners to report back by mid-2026 on progress rolling out missing middle housing - garden suites, multiplexes and small apartment buildings on major streets - following the Planning and Housing Committee's recommendation. City research estimates these housing types could deliver about 54,600 new units, roughly one-fifth of the 285,000 homes Toronto needs by 2031.

title: From Concept to Construction: Creating More Homes Across the Housing Continuum
brief: Housing starts are at historic lows, and of more than 230 affordable housing projects approved for city financial incentives, only 43 are under construction. Council is asked to direct staff, including through confidential instructions, to help move projects from planning to construction and occupancy. The report references figures of $85.7 million, $85,718,027, $16.9 million, $67.2 million, $67,199,200, $13 million, $596 million, $500 million, $800 million, $6.5, $8 billion and $60 million.

title: Advancing Six Sites for the Homelessness Services Capital Infrastructure Strategy (HSCIS) - City-Initiated Official Plan Amendment and Six Zoning By-law Amendments - Decision Report - Approval
topics: housing services, official plan amendments, rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Six city shelter sites could be rezoned to allow about 420 new shelter beds, with the buildings designed so they can later be converted to supportive or affordable housing. The sites are 1615 Dufferin Street; 2204-2212 Eglinton Avenue West and 601 Caledonia Road; 2535 Gerrard Street East; 68 Sheppard Avenue West; 66-66Y Third Street; and 1220-1222 Wilson Avenue. Council decides on the Official Plan and zoning amendments as part of the city's plan to add 1,600 new shelter spaces by 2033. The wider Homelessness Services Capital Infrastructure Strategy is estimated to cost $674.5 million over the ten-year capital planning period (2024–2033).

title: 3725 Bloor Street West - City-initiated Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
topics: development, mixed use areas, rezoning; developing land; development (land); land development, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: A city-owned site at 3725 Bloor Street West in Etobicoke could get a 43-storey mixed-use tower with about 698 rental homes, including 230 affordable units, plus an 804-square-metre public courtyard. Council decides whether to approve the city-initiated zoning change. The project is part of the city's Toronto Builds program for affordable housing on city-owned land near transit.

title: City Foundation Drainage Policy
topics: development review process, drainage areas, natural drainage systems; development control; development reviews, sewersheds
brief: Rules that require developers to manage groundwater on-site rather than discharging it into city sewers could be revisited. Council is asked to have Toronto Water and Development Review consult with industry and report back in early 2026 on possible changes to the Foundation Drainage Policy. Watertight basement requirements add costs, particularly to smaller and mid-rise buildings, which affects the cost of housing.

title: 324 Old Yonge Street - Notice of Intention to Designate a Property under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act
topics: heritage designation, heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: The 1935 Georgian Revival house at 324 Old Yonge Street in the St. Andrews-Windfields area of North York — the Jephcott-Sanderson Residence, designed by Allward and Guinlock — could begin heritage designation. Council decides whether to state its intention to designate under the Ontario Heritage Act. If no objections come in, the formal designation by-law can follow.

title: 21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 31, 33, 35, and 37 Kensington Avenue - Notice of Intention to Designate a Property under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act
topics: heritage designation, heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: Nine adjoining 19th-century buildings at 21 through 37 Kensington Avenue in Kensington Market — including 1880s Bay-and-Gable row houses — could begin heritage designation. Council decides whether to state its intention to designate the properties under the Ontario Heritage Act. If no objections come in, the formal designation by-law can follow.

title: 667 King Street West - Proposed Designation By-Law under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act - Consideration of Objection
topics: heritage designation, heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: Toronto's oldest bar, the Wheat Sheaf Tavern at 667 King Street West — a pre-Confederation inn built in 1849 at King and Bathurst — was flagged for heritage designation in March 2025, and the owner objected. Council must decide by July 29, 2025 whether to affirm the designation and pass the formal by-law. Staff maintain the property meets the provincial designation criteria.

title: 877 and 885 Lawrence Avenue East - Proposed Designation By-law Under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act - Consideration of Objection
topics: heritage designation, heritage preservation; historic preservation; historical preservation
brief: The two former bank branches at 877 and 885 Lawrence Avenue East in Don Mills — the 1956 Bank of Montreal and Bank of Nova Scotia pavilion buildings — were slated for heritage designation in March 2025, but the owner objected. Council must decide by July 29, 2025 whether to affirm the designation and pass the formal by-law. Staff say the properties meet the provincial criteria for designation despite the objection.

title: Expanding Housing Options in Neighbourhoods - Garden Suites Monitoring Program - Final Report
topics: housing, rezoning; homes; residences, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Rules for garden suites — small detached homes built in backyards behind existing houses — could be relaxed again following a city monitoring program. Council decides on Official Plan and zoning changes that also align city rules with recent provincial changes. Garden suites add housing options in residential neighbourhoods for households such as multigenerational families, renters and people aging in place.

title: 133 and 141 Erskine Avenue - Rental Housing Demolition Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: demolitions, development, rental housing; developing land; development (land); land development, rental properties; rental units
brief: Staff recommend approving the demolition of 26 rental homes at 133 Erskine Avenue, to be replaced in a new 35-storey, 364-home building that the Ontario Land Tribunal approved through a settlement in June 2024. The proposal includes a tenant assistance plan with a right of return at similar rents and financial compensation for hardship. City Council is being asked to approve the demolition. The item's source material also references $20,000.00.

title: 1410 Eglinton Avenue West - Zoning By-law Amendment - Appeal Report
topics: buildings, by-laws, zoning; bylaws
brief: A 43-storey building (145.25 metres plus penthouse) with 442 homes and ground-floor shops is proposed at 1410 Eglinton Avenue West. The applicant appealed the zoning amendment to the Ontario Land Tribunal in May 2025, after filing the application in January 2025, and North York Community Council is being asked to direct the City Solicitor to oppose the appeal at the hearing.

title: 272, 284, 286, 288, 290 and 296 Lawrence Avenue West and 1507, 1525, 1537, 1539, 1545 and 1549 Avenue Road - Rental Housing Demolition Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: demolitions, rental housing, tenants; rental properties; rental units, renters; tenancy agreements
brief: Staff recommend approving the demolition of 15 rental homes at 284 Lawrence Avenue West, to be replaced as part of a new development the Ontario Land Tribunal approved in principle: two mixed-use buildings of 12 and 14 storeys with 665 homes, including 15 replacement rental units. The proposal includes a tenant assistance plan with a right of return at similar rents and financial compensation for hardship. City Council is being asked to approve the demolition. The item's source material also references $20,000.00.

title: 2674-2704 Yonge Street and 19 Alexandra Boulevard - Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
topics: buildings, official plan amendments, rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend approving a 13-storey seniors residence (50.4 metres plus a 6-metre penthouse) at 2674-2704 Yonge Street and 19 Alexandra Boulevard, with 251 units including independent, assisted-living and memory-care suites. The plan includes 31 rental replacement units, a 205-square-metre addition to Snider Parkette and 370 square metres of publicly accessible open space, plus a tenant assistance plan giving existing tenants the right to return at similar rents. City Council is being asked to approve the Official Plan and zoning changes. The item's source material also references $950,000.00.

title: 123 Garratt Boulevard - Inclusion on the Heritage Register
topics: buildings, heritage properties, multi-unit dwellings; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties, multi residential apartment buildings; multi residential buildings; multi unit buildings; multi unit dwellings; multi-residential apartment buildings; multi-residential buildings; multi-unit buildings; multi-unit residential buildings; residential multi unit dwellings; residential multi-unit dwellings
brief: The former aircraft manufacturing complex at 123 Garratt Boulevard, in the southwestern part of the Downsview Area Secondary Plan, is recommended for the city's Heritage Register for its cultural heritage value. Listing would flag the buildings as historically significant and require the owner to give the city notice before any demolition. City Council makes the final call on listings.

title: 123 Garratt Boulevard (Taxiway West District) - Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
topics: development, mixed use areas, rezoning; developing land; development (land); land development, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend approving a large mixed-use development at 123 Garratt Boulevard in the Taxiway West District: about 489,009 square metres of floor area, including 282,750 square metres of non-residential space and 2,957 homes, with 10 percent of the residential floor area as affordable rental housing. The proposal also includes new parks and streets. City Council is being asked to approve the zoning change.

title: Renaming of Balmoral Park to Michael Mostyn Park
topics: facility naming, naming, parks and open space areas; green spaces; open spaces, park naming
brief: Balmoral Park would be renamed Michael Mostyn Park, honouring Michael Mostyn, the community leader and human rights advocate who died in February 2025. The park was chosen after consultation with city staff, residents, community organizations and his family. City Council is being asked to approve the renaming.

title: 47 Stadacona Drive and 22, 24, 26 and 28 Richlieu Road - Rental Housing Demolition Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: demolitions, housing, rentals; homes; residences
brief: Staff recommend approving the demolition of 11 rental homes in five single-storey detached buildings at 47 Stadacona Drive and 22, 24, 26 and 28 Richlieu Road. The 11 units would be replaced with 13 new ones, resized to meet the city's family-sized-unit guidelines, and the approval would carry conditions to protect current tenants. North York Community Council is being asked to decide the application. The item's source material also references $20,000.00.

title: Dedicate Lands as Public Highway to Form Part of Esther Shiner Boulevard, Provost Drive, and McMahon Drive
topics: highways, services, transportation; freeways; motorways; parkways, transportation services
brief: This is a technical item: land along Esther Shiner Boulevard, Provost Drive and McMahon Drive would be formally dedicated as public highway so the city can maintain it. Dedicating land for highway purposes needs full council sign-off, so City Council, not the community council, is being asked to approve it.

title: 47 Stadacona Drive and 22, 24, 26 and 28 Richelieu Road - Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
brief: Staff recommend approving a 12-storey mixed-use building with 190 homes and 550 square metres of shops at 47 Stadacona Drive and 22, 24, 26 and 28 Richelieu Road, with a holding provision on the zoning. The plan includes 13 replacement rental units. City Council is being asked to approve the zoning change.

title: Keele Street and Whitburn Crescent / Downsview Park Boulevard - Traffic Control Signal Modifications
topics: residential properties, signal controllers, traffic; controller units; fixed-time controllers; pretimed controllers; traffic-actuated controller, motor vehicle traffic; motorized traffic; traffic conditions; traffic flow; trip info; tripinfo, residential real estate
brief: Traffic signals at Keele Street and Whitburn Crescent / Downsview Park Boulevard are up for modification. The changes follow construction of a new public road, Downsview Park Boulevard, serving a new residential subdivision east of Keele Street; because the TTC runs transit on both streets, City Council approval is required. The signals manage vehicle flow and give pedestrians a safe crossing.

title: 30-36 Hendon Avenue - Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Refusal
topics: multi-unit dwellings, official plan amendments, rezoning; multi residential apartment buildings; multi residential buildings; multi unit buildings; multi unit dwellings; multi-residential apartment buildings; multi-residential buildings; multi-unit buildings; multi-unit residential buildings; residential multi unit dwellings; residential multi-unit dwellings, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend refusing a 46-storey, 433-home residential building at 30-36 Hendon Avenue, saying its height, scale and massing do not fit the site; the floor space would be 22.9 times the lot area. North York Community Council is being asked to adopt the refusal, keeping the current rules for the site.

title: 240-242 Finch Avenue West - Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: multi-unit dwellings, rezoning, zoning bylaws; multi residential apartment buildings; multi residential buildings; multi unit buildings; multi unit dwellings; multi-residential apartment buildings; multi-residential buildings; multi-unit buildings; multi-unit residential buildings; residential multi unit dwellings; residential multi-unit dwellings, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: Staff recommend approving a four-storey, purpose-built rental building with 41 homes at 240-242 Finch Avenue West. The proposal fits the Central Finch Area Secondary Plan, and City Council is being asked to amend the zoning by-law to allow it.

title: 110 Sheppard Avenue East - Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Refusal
topics: Official Plans, development, official plan amendments, zoning bylaws; developing land; development (land); land development, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: Staff recommend refusing a proposal at 110 Sheppard Avenue East for two buildings on a shared podium, 49 and 53 storeys with 1,313 homes. North York Community Council is being asked to adopt the refusal, which would leave the site's current land-use rules in place.

title: 5799-5915 Yonge Street and 46 and 47 Averill Crescent - Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: land, official plan amendments, rezoning; property, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend approving changes for 5799-5915 Yonge Street and 46 and 47 Averill Crescent: non-residential uses could expand above the second storey, and a requirement for 10,000 square metres of office space would become 10,000 square metres of non-residential space instead. City Council is being asked to approve the Official Plan and zoning amendments, along with changes to the site's Section 37 agreement.

title: 221-237 Finch Avenue West and 43 Finchurst Drive Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment Applications - Decision Report - Approval
topics: applications, official plan amendments, rezoning; application process, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend approving an 11-storey building (36 metres, plus a 5-metre mechanical penthouse) at 221-237 Finch Avenue West and 43 Finchurst Drive, with a holding provision attached to the zoning. The ground floor would have shops and live-work units facing Finch Avenue West. City Council is being asked to approve the Official Plan and zoning changes that would allow it.

title: Appointment of Public Members to the Toronto Community Housing Corporation Board of Directors
topics: public appointments;
brief: This is a procedural item: the Corporations Nominating Panel would recommend seven public members to City Council for appointment to the Toronto Community Housing Corporation Board of Directors, for terms ending July 26, 2027, and recommend a chair from among the public members and tenant directors. Confidential attachments would stay confidential. No policy change is proposed.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to the Transportation Services Division for the Reconstruction of the Rosedale Valley Multi-Use Trail - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: reconstruction, trail systems, transportation (sc); footpaths; multi-pupose trails; multi-purpose paths; multi-use pathways; multi-use trails; pedestrian trails; recreational trails; trail networks; trails; walking paths; waterfront trail, rebuilding
brief: The Rosedale Valley multi-use trail between Bayview Avenue and Park Road would be rebuilt to current safety, width and lighting standards with $2,483,625.13 in developer community benefits. Council would add $2,483,625.13 gross ($0 debt) to the Transportation Services capital budget, fully funded by Section 37 and 45 benefits — $142,858.14 from 590 Jarvis Street plus $571,432.53, $169,334.46 and $1,600,000.00 from other area developments — after tender costs came in too high to deliver the project without the supplement; the funds from 590 Jarvis Street have been dormant since 2005. The trail is uneven, narrow and poorly lit with a hazardous blind corner and no safe exit for cyclists at Park Road. Pedestrians and cyclists commuting between the Yonge Street area and the Don Valley would use the rebuilt trail.

title: Authorization to Terminate the 1992 Social Housing Agreement for 285-291 Jarvis Street Between the City of Toronto and Toronto Community Housing Corporation - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
topics: social housing; community housing; housing allowance; housing projects; low income housing; non profit housing; non-profit housing; public housing; rent geared to income assistance; rent geared to income housing; rent subsidies; rent supplement; subsidized housing; subsidized rent; subsidized units
brief: This is a procedural item: Council would terminate the 1992 social housing agreement for 285-291 Jarvis Street when the property transfers from Toronto Community Housing to Homes First Society in September 2025, and sign a modernized agreement. The property has been operated by Homes First for over 30 years as supportive housing for adult men with mental health and substance use challenges; the 1992 agreement, under the 1988 City of Toronto Act (No. 2), is outdated and inconsistent with the Tenants First direction to preserve long-term affordability under current legislation. The transfer was approved in 2018. Residents of the supportive housing are the ones affected.

title: Re-Opening and Amending Item 2025.EY20.2 - 56, 58 and 60 Fieldway Road - Community Benefits Charge In-Kind Report - by Councillor Amber Morley, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: development, zoning bylaws; developing land; development (land); land development, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: This is a technical amendment: Council would raise the developer's required on-site public art contribution at 56, 58 and 60 Fieldway Road from 33 percent to 55 percent of the community benefits charge amount. The four-tower mixed-use development's 2023 approval set the in-kind art contribution at up to 33 percent of 4 percent of land value; staff now say up to 55 percent is needed to realize the public art plan, with the rest of the charge paid at building permit issuance. Reopening item 2025.EY20.2 is required. The change affects the developer's art spending and the public art delivered on site.

title: Speeding up Transit in Ward 11 - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: parking fees, public transit; local transit; mass transit; public transport; public transportation; surface transit; transit; transit services; urban transportation, parking charges; parking rates
brief: On-street parking prices along busy Ward 11 bus and streetcar routes could be reset to discourage long-term parking and speed up surface transit. Council would have the Toronto Parking Authority report on setting rates on routes like Bathurst Street — where consultations showed parked cars slow buses and streetcars — plus reviewing parking times and turn permissions on local streets. The motion cites the Toronto Board of Trade's recommendation to use parking prices to redirect parking off arterial roads. Riders on Ward 11 surface routes would benefit if transit moves faster.

title: Request the Federal Government to Restore 100 Percent of the Funding to Shelter and Support Refugee Claimants - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Lily Cheng
topics: federal governments, refugees;
brief: Toronto would repeat its request that Ottawa cover the full cost of sheltering refugee claimants and build a coordinated national system for new arrivals. Council would ask the federal government to restore 100 percent of the funding and set up the national response, rather than winding down support — citing $1.1 billion the federal government has spent housing asylum claimants in hotels since 2017 and another $1.5 billion to provinces and cities through the Interim Housing Assistance Program. The motion quotes a federal briefing paper saying housing asylum claimants is provincial/municipal responsibility, with federal hotel funding as an emergency backstop since 2017, and calls the planned scale-back concerning. The City's shelter system and the claimants it houses are the ones affected.

title: Potential Future Community Recreation Centre in Liberty Village - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
topics: planning & development (sc), recreational facilities; recreation facilities; recreational amenities
brief: The question of a new community recreation centre in Liberty Village would stay in the planning process. Council would keep studying the need for the centre as part of the Liberty for All planning study — which will update the Garrison Common North Secondary Plan, expected at Council in the first quarter of 2026 — alongside Parks and Recreation's new city-wide Facilities Plan. The study, started in 2024, builds on the Liberty Village Public Realm Strategy, the Traffic Action Plan and ongoing engagement. Liberty Village residents would be the ones using any future centre.

title: Requesting Legal Review of Bid Process Complaint Relating to Toronto Parking Authority RFP-PARCS-202407 - by Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: parking, purchasing, quotations; acquisition; buying; procurement; sourcing; tenders, bids; quotes; request for quotation; rfq
brief: The City Manager and City Solicitor would review the Toronto Parking Authority's bidding process for a new parking payment system after a bidder filed a complaint. Council would request the legal and policy compliance review of the Parking Access and Revenue Control System procurement (RFP-PARCS-202407) — replacing a 25-year-old system — and a report back by late 2025. The motion is urgent because no council meeting is scheduled until late September and the procurement is underway. The outcome would affect how the parking authority runs its payment system.

title: Creating More Affordable Housing Options in Our Neighbourhoods - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
topics: urban planning, zoning; city planning; community planning; regional planning
brief: Builders of multiplexes with up to six homes could see development charges waived on the second, third and fourth units. Council would amend Municipal Code Chapter 415 so the first four units in developments of up to six units get the same exemption that multiplexes of four units and under already have, and direct the Chief Planner to consider permeable paving options for suburban wards with windrow-clearing services as part of soft landscaping requirements. The motion says rising costs are putting Scarborough-style multigenerational homes out of reach. Families looking for affordable multigenerational housing would be the intended beneficiaries.

title: Assistance to the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul’s Project at 21-31 Windsor Street, 18 Buckingham Street, 60 Newcastle Street and 95 Portland Street - by Councillor Amber Morley, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: zoning, zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The Society of Saint Vincent de Paul's shelter project near King and Dufferin would get site plan application fees waived, with a staff report on extending the break to building permit fees and development charges. Council would waive the fees for the project at 21-31 Windsor Street, 18 Buckingham Street, 60 Newcastle Street and 95 Portland Street, which includes a seven-storey women's shelter with 36 supportive dwelling units, 16 emergency shelter beds and 72 shelter beds (Building C) replacing the existing Elisa House. Council previously waived fees and exemptions for the supportive units through the Open Door program, but technicalities excluded the shelter portion. The decision would affect the project's costs and the women it would house.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to The Humber Bay Park East Shoreline Design Improvements - by Councillor Amber Morley, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: conservation authorities, parks; conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland
brief: Design improvements to the shoreline at Humber Bay Park East would get $155,000.00 in developer community benefits. Council would release the Section 37 funds for the redesign work, following residents' concerns that the Humber Bay Park Master Plan construction — done with the Toronto and Region Conservation Authority — replaced the accessible beach with large cobble stones and restricted water access, despite consultation impressions from 2016-2019 that the beach would remain. The motion balances shoreline resilience against erosion, extreme weather and climate change with recreation and amenities. Beachgoers and nearby residents are the ones affected.

title: 125 The Esplanade - Interim Park Implementation - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: buildings, farmer, sporting events; championships
brief: A temporary park would be created at 125 The Esplanade once the temporary North St. Lawrence Market building is removed. Council would ask Parks and Recreation to implement interim park use and beautification at the site — designated as a future park since 2016, when the temporary market building went up — timed with the structure's decommissioning and ahead of the FIFA World Cup 2026. The new North Market building opened in May 2025, and planning for the site's long-term future continues alongside the David Crombie Park revitalization starting in 2025. The St. Lawrence community would keep a public space in the meantime.

title: Working Collaboratively Towards a Positive Outcome for the Future Indigenous Women and Children’s Shelter at 68 Sheppard Avenue West by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: First Nations, women; aboriginal community; aboriginal peoples; aboriginals; indians (native); indigenous peoples; inuit; metis; métis; native peoples, shelters for women
brief: The City could buy properties next to 68 Sheppard Avenue West to support Toronto's first City-led Indigenous Women and Children's Shelter. Council would ask shelter and real estate staff, with CreateTO, to consider acquiring adjacent sites in connection with the shelter development, weighing key program criteria developed with the shelter provider, the Native Women's Resource Centre of Toronto. The Willowdale site's implementation is underway. The decision would affect the shelter's capacity and the surrounding properties.

title: Accepting In-Kind Donation from Scarborough Cricket Association for Facility Improvements at Milliken Park - by Councillor Jamaal Myers, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
topics: cricket, donation, parks; bequest; toy drive, conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland
brief: Milliken Park could get a cricket pitch and/or batting cages built with up to $150,000 in donated work from the Scarborough Cricket Association. Council would accept the in-kind donation — valued at up to $0.150 million, above the $0.050 million threshold requiring Council authority — and add $0.150 million to the 2025 Parks and Recreation capital budget, with no costs to the division and ongoing maintenance covered by its operating budget. The motion is urgent to keep consultations, design and a 2026 opening on track and protect donor commitments. Local cricket players would be the main users.

title: 250 Wincott Drive - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Ontario Land Tribunal - by Councillor Stephen Holyday, seconded by Councillor Parthi Kandavel
topics: zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The City would take the Ontario Land Tribunal to support the Committee of Adjustment's refusal of parking and loading variances for a large development at 250 Wincott Drive. Council would authorize the City Solicitor to attend the OLT to back the refusal of the four variances for a proposed new building on the east side of the site — part of a multi-building mixed-use development first approved in 2021, now seeking reduced parking and increased heights. The owner has also applied for a zoning amendment for taller buildings on the west side, now under staff review. The Tribunal outcome would shape the development's parking and scale.

title: Bluffer’s Park Action Plan - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Nick Mantas
topics: park maintenance, recreation & tourism (sc); parks maintenance
brief: Bluffer's Park would get a holistic action plan of priority environmental and physical improvements ahead of its 50th anniversary. Council would direct parks staff, working with conservation authorities and the community, to develop the plan to address heavy use, aging facilities and repeated storm and flood damage at the Scarborough waterfront park. The motion is framed as timely, with capital projects like the Brimley Road multi-use trail starting this autumn. The plan would shape renewal of the park for Scarborough and the wider city.

title: 42 Donalda Crescent - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Nick Mantas, seconded by Councillor Paul Ainslie
topics: zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The City would appeal the Committee of Adjustment's approval of a one-storey rear-yard garden suite at 42 Donalda Crescent. Council would authorize the City Solicitor to appeal the Scarborough District panel's approval of variances for the height and lot coverage of the ancillary building, and to oppose the development at the Toronto Local Appeal Body — even though planning staff had recommended approval with conditions and Urban Forestry added one condition, and the Committee approved it on July 15, 2025. The motion also covers hiring outside consultants and negotiating a settlement. The appeal would decide whether the garden suite proceeds as approved.

title: 131 McCormack Street - Request for City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: zoning, zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The City would appeal the Committee of Adjustment's approval of an entertainment venue at 131 McCormack Street. Council would authorize the City Solicitor to appeal the July 10, 2025 decision that legalized the existing Entertainment Place of Assembly for two years (expiring July 31, 2027), and to oppose the variance at the Toronto Local Appeal Body. Planning staff had said the change of use was not minor and would require a zoning by-law amendment in the Employment Industrial zone, recommending the two-year limit if approved. The motion also lets the Solicitor hire consultants and negotiate a settlement.

title: Keeping our Sidewalks Clear - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
topics: pedestrian walkways, sidewalks; footpaths; pedestrian ways; walking paths; walkways
brief: Food-delivery e-bikes and scooters blocking sidewalks would be studied for short- and long-term fixes. Council would have staff examine how micromobility traffic from apps like Uber, DoorDash and Skip affects sidewalk access — especially for people with strollers and wheelchairs — and report on solutions, after reported conflicts rose sharply this summer. The motion says delivery vehicles congregate on sidewalks waiting for orders, blocking pedestrians and shoppers. Pedestrians, local businesses and delivery workers would all be affected by whatever rules follow.

title: Re-opening and Amending Item 2025.PH21.9 - Providing Housing Opening Today Toronto Inc., with Section 37 Funds for Purchase of Affordable Rental Housing Building - by Councillor Gord Perks, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: rental housing; rental properties; rental units
brief: The wording of Council's earlier decision giving Section 37 funds to Housing Opening Today Toronto to buy a rental building would be widened so the building can become affordable over time. Council would amend item 2025.PH21.9 to clarify that the Ward 4 Parkdale-High Park property — which includes apartments currently rented above the City's affordable definition — qualifies, since rents will transition down to affordable levels as tenants move out and new eligible tenants move in, and current tenants will be income-tested. The item's figures list $1,500,000.00, broken into $205,966.27, $478,208.82 and $815,824.91. Existing tenants would keep their homes while the building moves toward full affordability.

title: Removal of Section 118 Notice of Restrictions from Title to 429 Pape Avenue - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Frances Nunziata
topics: construction, land use; building
brief: This is a procedural item: Council would remove a Section 118 land-title notice on 429 Pape Avenue so Metrolinx can buy the property for Ontario Line construction without a formal expropriation. Metrolinx has registered a Certificate of Approval against the property and offered to buy it from Wigwamen Incorporated, which received it — with 19 other houses — as affordable housing in 2010; the notice bars transfers for 25 years without City consent. Removing it would let the sale close by the end of July 2025 and maximize sale proceeds. No policy change is involved.

title: Bloordale Village Business Improvement Area - 2025 Operating Budget - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
topics: operating budgets;
brief: This is a procedural item: Council would approve the Bloordale Village Business Improvement Area's 2025 operating budget of $285,000 and its $163,000 levy, funded by a special charge on local commercial and industrial properties. The City of Toronto Act, 2006 requires Council to approve each BIA's annual budget. No City funding is involved; the levy was not on the regular property bills because of the timing of the BIA's annual general meeting.

title: Accepting an Award From Bloomberg Philanthropies as Part of the Finalist Stage of the 2025 Global Mayors Challenge - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos-Lin
topics: awards;
brief: Toronto would accept a USD $50,000 award (CAD $68,500) from Bloomberg Philanthropies as a finalist in the 2025 Global Mayors Challenge, to refine its proposal for a universal school food program. Council would authorize acceptance of the award — Toronto was the only Canadian city among 50 finalists chosen from over 630 applicants — with the money used for expert coaching and a submission to the final round in October 2025; 25 finalists will then receive USD $1,000,000 (about CAD $1.37 million) to implement their ideas. City and Mayor's Office staff would attend the Global Ideas Camp in Bogota, Colombia, in July 2025. The work ties to the school food program vision Council approved in June 2025.

title: CityServeTO - A Youth-based Community Service Initiative - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Jon Burnside
topics: community development, youth; adolescents, community building; community capacity building; community engagement; social development
brief: Two community health centres would each get up to $700,000 to run the first cycle of CityServeTO, a youth community service program. Council would fund Scarborough Centre for Healthy Communities and Rexdale Community Health Centre for the September 2025 to June 2026 cycle of the program, co-developed by the Youth Development Unit as part of the Mayor's Youth Safety Task Force, offering paid team-based service, mentorship and job readiness support to youth aged 16-24 most affected by violence, poverty and exclusion. The program includes potential placements in City divisions. Young people in Scarborough and Rexdale would get the paid opportunities.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Design and Construct New and Expanded Sports Courts at Clairlea Park - by Councillor Parthi Kandavel, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
topics: basketball, parks, sports; conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland
brief: Clairlea Park would get new and expanded sports courts — including pickleball and basketball — under a $67,412.88 capital project funded by developer money. Council would redirect Section 37 benefits for the design and construction at 45 Fairfax Crescent in the Clairlea-Birchmount neighbourhood, less than 2 kilometres from the 0 Hymus Road development; the item's figures break the total into $10,000 and $57,412.88, and into $11,349.88 and $56,063. The park currently has two tennis courts and an underutilized sports pad, and community engagement would shape the final court layout. Pickleball players and local families would use the upgraded courts, with funds to be spent in 2025-2026.

title: Request for City-Initiated Zoning By-law Amendment 1049-2022 to Re-allocate Section 37 Funds - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
topics: funding, zoning bylaws; financing, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: $250,000 in unspent developer funds from the 91-101 Raglan development would be redirected from public art to streetscape improvements in the Bathurst-St. Clair area. Council would re-allocate the Section 37 money — secured by Zoning By-law 1049-2022 in 2022 for a public art contribution that was never spent, and redirectable after three years — toward the streetscape and public realm master plan for Raglan Avenue being finalized by Transportation Services and City Planning. The motion says the apartment neighbourhood is seeing the greatest volume of development and needs the public realm investment. Residents along Raglan Avenue would see the improvements.

title: Off-Site Parkland Dedication for 289 to 299 Balliol Street and 305 Balliol Street - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
brief: The developer of a 31-storey mixed-use project at 289 to 299 Balliol Street and 305 Balliol Street would be asked to find off-site parkland to give the City instead of paying cash-in-lieu. Council would authorize staff to work with the owner to seek and accept an off-site parkland dedication — or cash-in-lieu as the alternative — under Section 42 of the Planning Act, following the Ontario Land Tribunal's January 2025 final order on the zoning amendment. The owner has indicated it prefers off-site dedication. Parks staff need the approval to direct the acquisition within specific agreement deadlines.

title: 850 Carlaw Avenue - Liquor Licence Application - Dopapen Coffee - License Number 3213857 - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
topics: food service establishments, liquor sales licences; alcohol permits; liquor licences; liquor permits, burger shops; coffee shops; delicatessens; donut shops; eating establishments; fast food outlets; fish and chips shops; food premises; pizza parlours; restaurants (businesses)
brief: City Council would tell Ontario's alcohol regulator that a liquor licence for Dopapen Coffee at 850 Carlaw Avenue is not in the public interest unless residents' concerns are addressed. Council would direct the City Clerk to advise the Registrar of the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario to issue a Proposal to Review or Refuse the indoor-only licence application, citing neighbourhood concerns about noise, litter, safety and lighting in the low-density residential area. The matter is urgent because the objection deadline is August 5, 2025. The decision on the licence rests with the AGCO.

title: Renaming of Diamond 1 at Wishing Well Park as “Darryl Harding Memorial Diamond” - by Councillor Nick Mantas, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: baseball diamonds, memorials; ball diamonds; baseball fields; hardball diamonds, monuments; permanent memorials
brief: Diamond 1 at Wishing Well Park would be renamed the Darryl Harding Memorial Diamond, honouring the longtime Scarborough youth baseball coach and mentor who died in August 2024. Council would approve the naming for Harding — known as Coach D — who as president and coach of the Wexford Agincourt Baseball League volunteered over 1,200 hours a year, helped create a girls-only division with the Jays Care Foundation Rookie League, and covered registration fees for children from low-income families. Community organizations, residents and local leaders were consulted on the proposal. Young players at the park would play on a diamond bearing his name.

title: Re-opening and Amending Item 2025.CC31.10 - 2346 Yonge Street - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions - by Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
topics: hearings, planning tribunals; omb; ontario municipal board
brief: This is a procedural item: Council would reopen its June 2025 decision on the 2346 Yonge Street Ontario Land Tribunal appeal (item 2025.CC31.10) to fix the confidentiality wording. The amendment changes references from Confidential Appendices A and B to Confidential Appendix A, so that one attachment stays confidential while the staff instructions in the other can be released publicly. Legal Services advised the change. No policy or development decision is altered.

title: Authority to Accept a Donation and Enter Into an Agreement for Baseball Diamond Improvements at Christie Pits Park - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Paul Ainslie
topics: donation, parks, recreational facilities; bequest; toy drive, conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland, recreation facilities; recreational amenities
brief: Baseball Diamond 2 at Christie Pits Park would get up to $190,000 in donated upgrades from the Toronto Playgrounds Baseball League. Council would accept the donation and enter an agreement for the improvements — funded by a $100,000 bequest from the Dominico family and a $90,000 Jays Care Foundation grant, with the item's figures also listing $50,000 — and Parks and Recreation staff would lead design and construction, targeting completion in October 2025. Planned work includes converting the infield to Mar-Co Clay, water spigots, better accessibility behind the backstop, realigned bleachers and dugouts, and drainage work. Children and youth in the league's baseball programming are the main users.

title: Authorization to Release Section 45 Funds from the Developments at 4726-4728 Yonge Street, 9-31 Bogert Avenue and 2-28 Poyntz Avenue for the Capital Improvements to the Schoolyard at Avondale Public School - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor James Pasternak
topics: funding, playgrounds, public schools; adventure playgrounds; indoor playgrounds; playground structures, financing
brief: The schoolyard at Avondale Public School would get $50,000.00 in developer funds toward upgrades including a pollinator garden, a turfed soccer field and an improved playscape with seating and shade. Council would release the Section 45 funds from developments at 4726-4728 Yonge Street, 9-31 Bogert Avenue and 2-28 Poyntz Avenue to the Toronto District School Board for the capital improvements. The school, rebuilt in 2019, already serves about 1,000 students — well beyond its 861 capacity — and the yard is a key outdoor space for the 14,400 people living within a 5-10 minute walk. Students and neighbours using the yard evenings and weekends would benefit.

title: Temporary Delegation: Authority During the Summer Recess to Direct Attendance on Appeals of Committee of Adjustment Decisions - by Councillor Gord Perks, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: delegation of authority; signing authorities
brief: This is a procedural item: Council would temporarily delegate authority to the Executive Director of Development Review to instruct the City Solicitor on Committee of Adjustment appeals during the summer recess, from the July 23-25, 2025 council meeting until October 8-10, 2025. The delegation covers attending the Toronto Local Appeal Body (or Ontario Land Tribunal where related), filing City appeals, hiring outside experts and resolving matters in consultation with the ward councillor. Without it, the City could miss legal deadlines on planning appeals while Council is not meeting. No policy change is involved.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Ward 13 2024 Participatory Budgeting Projects for Cabbagetown Neighbourhood - New Street Benches for Cabbagetown Business Improvement Area - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
topics: benches (street furniture), budgets; budgets and accounts
brief: Twenty-five new benches along Parliament, Carlton and Gerrard main streets would be installed for $46,800 in resident-voted developer funds. Council would add $46,800 gross ($0 net) to the 2025 Non-Program operating budget, drawn from the $750,000 Ward 13 participatory budgeting envelope, for the Cabbagetown BIA benches — one of nine winning projects that needed additional review. Residents chose the projects through 2024 voting. Shoppers and pedestrians on the three main streets would get the new seating.

title: Toronto City Council Support for CHIN Radio/TV International’s Canadian Radio-television Telecommunications Commission Application to Relocate its AM Broadcast Service to AM900 - by Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: mass media, telecommunications; broadcast media; media organizations; print media; web media, phone services; telephone services; voice communication; voice mail
brief: City Council would send a letter to the CRTC supporting CHIN Radio's application to move its AM broadcast to the AM900 frequency. The motion says CHIN Radio — a multicultural broadcaster approaching its 60th anniversary in 2026, programming in over 17 languages — lost its long-standing Toronto Islands transmitter site and moved to Halton Hills, hurting its signal quality and reach. Approving the frequency move would help restore the service for diverse audiences across the Greater Toronto and Hamilton area. The decision rests with the CRTC; Council's letter would be a show of support.

title: Re-Opening and Amending Item 2024.EX18.7 - CaféTO Business Improvement Area (BIA) Pilot Programs Update and Toronto Municipal Code Amendments for 2025 - by Councillor Brad Bradford, seconded by Councillor Stephen Holyday
topics: small businesses, street occupation permits; curblane permits; road use permits; street closure permits; streets and sidewalks
brief: CaféTO patio applications could only be refused when more than 25 percent of the notified members of the public object. Council would amend the 2025 CaféTO rules — reopening item 2024.EX18.7 — after the motion describes a Beach patio shut down for nearly two months over two objections during the 21-day notice period, and says the refusal process creates red tape for small businesses. The stated goal is simpler patio approvals. The change would affect restaurants and bars with sidewalk cafés and nearby residents who receive notice.

title: Accepting an In-Kind Donation from Valley Tennis Club for Improvements at York Mills Valley Park - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
topics: donation, sports clubs; badminton clubs; baseball associations; baseball leagues; bowling clubs; cross-country ski clubs; curling clubs; gymnastic clubs; hockey associations; hockey leagues; karate clubs; lacrosse clubs; lawn bowling clubs; ride clubs; rifle clubs; slo-pitch leagues; soccer clubs; soccer leagues; softball associations; softball leagues; swim clubs; tennis clubs; volleyball clubs, bequest; toy drive
brief: The Valley Tennis Club would fund and coordinate resurfacing of five City-owned tennis courts at York Mills Valley Park, with the donated work valued at $74,450.00 plus HST. Council would formally accept the in-kind donation and authorize the agreement so the club can start September 1, 2025 and finish in the fall, under the 2004 Policy for Community Tennis Club Operations (the earlier summary put the value at up to $90,000). The club has secured a quote for the work. Players using the public courts would get repaired playing surfaces.

title: Taking Action to Protect Tenants - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: rent, tenants; renters; tenancy agreements, rents
brief: Apartment buildings could get colour-coded RentSafe signs — red for serious health and safety violations, yellow for minor infractions, green for good repair — posted in a visible spot on each building and on the City website. Council would create the rating system, based on the City's RentSafeTO building scores and modelled on the DineSafe program. The motion says tenants support the signs — citing a 2020 City survey where 81 percent agreed — and groups including ACORN and tenant associations back them, while landlords have argued a red sign would stigmatize residents. Renters across Toronto would see the ratings when choosing where to live.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Support the Redesign of the Vale of Avoca Ravine to Include a Missing Walking Trail Connection - by Councillor Josh Matlow, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: ravines, trail systems; footpaths; multi-pupose trails; multi-purpose paths; multi-use pathways; multi-use trails; pedestrian trails; recreational trails; trail networks; trails; walking paths; waterfront trail, ravine protection areas
brief: The detailed design of a missing walking trail connection in the Vale of Avoca ravine would move ahead with $250,000 in developer community benefits from the 1331 Yonge Street development. Council would release the Section 37 funds for the redesign of the ravine near Yonge Street and St. Clair, where the ravine's trails, staircases and creek walls have deteriorated through erosion and neglect; the item's source figures also list $40 million, $1.5 million and $1 million for the wider ravine work, with the budget detail showing $250,000.00. The ravine straddles Wards 11 and 12 near subway Line 1. Hikers and nearby residents would gain the restored connection.

title: Strengthening Protections for Toronto's Tree Canopy - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
topics: tree canopy, tree protection; tree canopy cover; tree cover
brief: The City would develop stronger tools to protect trees covered by the tree by-law after a protected mature honey locust was removed without permits at a Leaside infill development site on June 25, 2025. Council would have planning and forestry staff build the protections, after the tree came down despite revised plans meant to save it and the applicant then resubmitted to add a parking pad. The motion says current recourse for by-law contraventions does not reflect the canopy's importance to health and the TransformTO emissions targets, and notes most potential canopy growth space is on private property. Property owners, developers and residents would face the new rules.

title: Entering into an Agreement with ArtHubs Toronto Inc. at Spectrum Park (Regent Park Boulevard Park) - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: agreements, parks; conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland, tenancy agreements
brief: ArtHubs Toronto Inc, would take over community programming at Spectrum Park in Regent Park under a three-year nominal-fee licence with the City. Council would authorize parks staff to sign the non-exclusive licence agreement for the 1,289-square-metre plaza at 81 Regent Park Boulevard, built for public programming as part of the Regent Park redevelopment. ArtHubs was established in late 2023 as the successor non-profit to Toronto Artscape Inc., which had managed the nearby Daniels Spectrum; the original 2023 agreement with Artscape was never fully executed. Community members using the park for events and programming would be affected.

title: Authority to Accept In-Kind Donation and Issue Tax Receipt - Dafoe Urn Restoration Project at Craigleigh Gardens Park - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Paul Ainslie
topics: donation, garden parks; bequest; toy drive
brief: A 19th-century cast-iron urn would be installed in Craigleigh Gardens Park as a donated heritage piece. Council would accept the in-kind donation of the Dafoe Urn — originally at St. Lawrence Hall and preserved by the family of Olympian Frances Dafoe — with restoration, transportation and installation costs covered by donors Blake Melnick ($33,117.31) and Adrian Dafoe ($25,098.00) in exchange for tax receipts; the earlier summary valued the donation at up to $65,000. The South Rosedale Residents' Association supports placing the urn in the heritage park in the South Rosedale neighbourhood. Park visitors would see the restored urn on public display.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for Vision Zero Streetscape Improvements at Redpath and Erskine and Erskine and Yonge - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
topics: infrastructure, road reconstruction; road alterations; road narrowing; road widening
brief: Two Midtown intersections would get road-safety upgrades bundled with planned summer resurfacing, for $239,311.40. Council would add $239,311.40 gross ($0 debt) to the Transportation Services capital budget, fully funded by Section 37 benefits from developments at 73-79 Keewatin Avenue, 88 Erskine Avenue, 101 Erskine Avenue and 66 Broadway Avenue — the item's figures break this into $27,691.58 and $211,619.82 — for geometric safety improvements at Redpath Avenue and Erskine Avenue, and Erskine Avenue and Yonge Street. The work is identified in the Midtown Infrastructure Implementation Strategy. Drivers, cyclists and pedestrians at the two intersections would use the safer layouts.

title: Authorization to Release Sections 37 Funds for Pedestrian Safety on Avenue Road - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: pedestrian signals; crosswalk lights; pedestrian displays
brief: A signalized pedestrian crossing would be built on Avenue Road between Davenport Road and Dupont Street for $200,000. Council would increase the Transportation Services capital budget by $200,000 gross ($0 net), fully funded by Section 37 benefits, for the mid-block crossing near 215 Avenue Road that Council authorized in 2024 and is now ready for construction. The Avenue Road Safety Coalition has long sought improvements on the stretch, which has narrow sidewalks and no convenient access from the intensifying west side to the new Ramsden Park entrance. Pedestrians crossing Avenue Road would be the direct beneficiaries.

title: Review of Automated Speed Enforcement (ASE) Ticket Appeals Process - by Councillor James Pasternak, seconded by Councillor Anthony Perruzza
topics: enforcement, tickets, traffic speed, traffic violations; demerit points; speeding tickets
brief: The process for disputing automated speed enforcement tickets would get a full review. Council would have court staff examine the ASE appeals process — after residents reported the website not recognizing ticket numbers, outdated email addresses on tickets, long phone hold times and poor communication on appeal status — and report back in October 2025 on making it straightforward and easy to navigate. The motion frames the review as protecting due process within the Vision Zero road safety strategy. Any driver appealing a speed-camera ticket would use the improved process.

title: Safer Shores at Woodbine Beach: Protecting the Safety of Our Waterfront and Everyone Who Enjoys It - by Councillor Brad Bradford, seconded by Councillor Jon Burnside
topics: beaches, recreational watercraft; boat launching; boats; leisure water vehicles; pleasure boats; pleasure craft
brief: Ports Toronto would be asked to create a no-go zone of at least 100 metres from the Woodbine Beach shoreline for motorized watercraft. Council would make the request to address safety concerns around unlicensed personal watercraft (Jet Ski) rental operators near swimmers and crowded beaches, after targeted enforcement blitzes by the Toronto Police Marine Unit this summer. The motion notes the City faced similar concerns in 2019 and responded with clarified swimming zones and safety signage. Swimmers and beachgoers at Woodbine Beach are the ones affected.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Support the Redesign of the Vale of Avoca Ravine to Include a Missing Walking Trail Connection - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: nature trails, ravines; interpretive trails; urban wilderness trails, ravine protection areas
brief: The detailed design of a new walking trail connection in the Vale of Avoca ravine would move ahead with $250,000 in developer community benefits. Council would release the Section 37 funds for the redesign of the ravine near Yonge Street and St. Clair, where Yellow Creek runs through steep, eroding valley walls and trails and staircases have deteriorated; the item's source figures also list $40 million, $1.5 million and $1 million for the wider ravine work. The ravine straddles Wards 11 and 12 in a rapidly intensifying area near subway Line 1. Hikers and nearby residents would gain a restored trail link through the valley.

title: No More Weeds and Tree Coffins Across our Public Right of Way - by Councillor Lily Cheng, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
topics: pedestrian walkways, weeds; footpaths; pedestrian ways; walking paths; walkways, grass and weeds; long grass; weeds and tall grass
brief: Responsibility for maintaining planters and landscaping on public property next to private developments could get clearer rules. Council would direct the Chief Planner and Executive Director of Development Review to include recommendations — on development approvals, design standards and stronger by-laws for who maintains these features — in the fourth-quarter 2025 report back to the Executive Committee requested under item 2025.EX22.3. The motion says unclear responsibility lets some streetscape elements fall into neglect, hurting their appearance and environmental value. Pedestrians and neighbours on streets with these features would see the difference.

title: Helping Evicted Tenants Access Shelter and Support - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
topics: eviction, social assistance, tenants; financial assistance; income assistance; ontario works; ow; welfare, renters; tenancy agreements
brief: Evicted Toronto tenants would get contact information for City housing resources when an eviction order is issued. Council would request that Ontario's Attorney General and the Landlord and Tenant Board provide tenants with details of applicable City resources, including the phone number for Central Intake, at the time of the order — the motion says the Board currently gives tenants no such information. The motion cites the recent case of 91-year-old Isidoro Ventullo, evicted after two decades in his apartment, who did not know where to turn until the sheriff arrived. Tenants facing eviction would get an earlier path to shelter and support services.

title: Amending an Encroachment Agreement with the University of Toronto to enable low Carbon District Energy - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Parthi Kandavel
topics: heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems; air conditioning; air conditioning systems; boilers; climate control systems; cooling systems; furnaces; heat; heating systems; hvac; ventilation; ventilation systems
brief: The University of Toronto would not have to pay the annual licence fee for the geothermal pipes serving its Oak House student residence. Council would waive the fee — appraised at $50,000 a year, indexed every five years — for the pipes in the public right of way connecting the geothermal system under Robert Street Field to Oak House at 700 Spadina Avenue and 54 Sussex Avenue, and have staff report in 2026 on a standard approach for such low-carbon energy projects. The university objected that the fee exceeds the pipes' construction cost and notes fossil fuel piping uses the right of way without payment by provincial law. The decision affects how the City treats low-carbon district energy in its streets.

title: Implementation Strategy for Business Improvement Area Streetscape Master Plans - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
topics: Master Plans, business improvement areas; bia; business improvement associations
brief: Business improvement area streetscape master plans could become official guidance for how Toronto's main streets are rebuilt. Council would have planning staff review BIA streetscape master plans and use the relevant details in the City's Streetscape Manual and when reviewing development applications, so visions funded partly by City grants are not lost when new development replaces sidewalks or capital work is planned. The motion cites three BIAs in Toronto Centre that have completed such plans. The change would affect how commercial streets get wider sidewalks, patios, safety improvements and green infrastructure as the city grows.

title: Accepting an In-Kind Donation from East York Tennis Club for Capital Improvement at Cosburn Park - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
topics: donation, sports clubs, tennis; badminton clubs; baseball associations; baseball leagues; bowling clubs; cross-country ski clubs; curling clubs; gymnastic clubs; hockey associations; hockey leagues; karate clubs; lacrosse clubs; lawn bowling clubs; ride clubs; rifle clubs; slo-pitch leagues; soccer clubs; soccer leagues; softball associations; softball leagues; swim clubs; tennis clubs; volleyball clubs, bequest; toy drive
brief: The five tennis courts at Cosburn Park would be refurbished with up to $400,000 in donated work from the East York Tennis Club. Council would accept the in-kind donation — funded from the club's capital reserve and delivered through a construction and donation agreement with Parks and Recreation — under the 2004 Policy for Community Tennis Club Operations, with work starting in fall 2025. The club operates the five hard courts at 115 Roosevelt Road in Cosburn Park, Ward 14. Players using the public courts would get resurfaced playing surfaces.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds from the Development at 1 Bloor Street West to St. Clare’s MultiFaith Housing to enhance accessibility and add recording space to the new performance centre at 877 Yonge Street - by Councillor Dianne Saxe, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
topics: accessibility, accessibility standards; accessibility legislation; aoda, barrier-free design; universal design; wheelchair accessible
brief: St. Clare's MultiFaith Housing would get $109,586 to improve accessibility and add recording space at the Jackman Performance Centre at 877 Yonge Street. Council would release the Section 37 funds from the development at 1 Bloor Street West to the housing agency, which manages the City-owned supportive housing above the theatre space created by Nightwood Theatre and Tapestry Opera; the work would add automatic door openers and a recording studio (Council would increase the operating budget by $150,000 gross at $0 net, forwarding $109,586 of it to St. Clare's). Previous Section 37 money fitted out the performance space and made much of it wheelchair accessible. Theatre artists, supportive housing tenants and the surrounding community use the centre.

title: Fossil Fuel Advocacy Advertising on City Assets
topics: advertising, city-owned properties, greenhouse effect; city owned properties; city properties, greenhouse gas emissions
brief: Developing a greenwashing statement for the City's website — and requiring advertisers on City assets to sign a declaration that their environmental claims are not false or misleading, while adding climate action messages to City advertising campaigns — goes to City Council for approval. The report follows 2024 concerns about fossil fuel advocacy advertising on TTC vehicles; it would not apply to ads for products that use fossil fuels, such as vehicles and appliances.

title: Approach to Public Electric Vehicle Charging Delivery Model
topics: agreements, climate, motor vehicles; tenancy agreements, vehicles
brief: Moving ahead with a collaborative model for building Toronto's public electric vehicle charging network, with Environment, Climate and Forestry and the Toronto Parking Authority negotiating with three short-listed companies and reporting back on results by early 2026 goes to City Council for approval. The plan supports TransformTO's goal of 30 per cent electric vehicle ownership by 2030; a three-year installation and funding strategy comes to Council in late 2025.

title: Temporary Ramps for Stepped Entrances - Amendments to Chapter 743
topics: municipal codes, sidewalks, wheelchair ramps; handicapped ramps
brief: Amending the streets and sidewalks by-law to allow businesses to place temporary accessibility ramps on sidewalks as permitted encroachments, so shops with stepped entrances can be made accessible to people using mobility devices goes to City Council for approval. The changes aim to balance accessibility with maintaining clear pedestrian pathways.

title: Cycling Network Plan - 2025 Cycling Infrastructure and Missing Sidewalk Installation - Second Quarter Update

title: Business Licence and Permit Applications Action Plan: Chapter 545, Licensing (2025 to 2029)
topics: business licences, permits; business licensing; business permits; municipal licenses, permit renewal
brief: A major overhaul of the city's business licensing bylaw goes to Council for approval. The item asks council to amend Toronto Municipal Code Chapter 545, Licensing, under the 2025-2029 Business Licence and Permit Applications Action Plan. Council is asked to delete four application requirements: filing lists of services and fees, filing lists of employees, limits on working for only one employer, and mandatory medical examinations. It would also remove municipal licensing entirely for seven trades — boats for hire, school bus drivers, transient traders, building cleaners, chimney repairmen, builders of radiation fall-out shelters, and collectors of second-hand goods — along with their application and renewal fees (ranging from $281.87 to $758.01). The plan would let Municipal Licensing and Standards place conditions on a business licence, alongside the Toronto Licensing Tribunal; require applicants to provide an email contact; update rules for commercial parking lots, laundries and driving schools; and add a new $239.11 zoning review fee per business licence application. The changes would take effect January 1, 2026, with existing licences for the removed trades extended to December 31, 2025 without renewal fees.

topics: Toronto Transit Commission, public transit, purchasing, specialized paratransit services; accessible public transportation; accessible transit; accessible transit service; door to door service; special mobility services; wheel trans; wheel-trans; wheeltrans, acquisition; buying; procurement; sourcing; tenders, local transit; mass transit; public transport; public transportation; surface transit; transit; transit services; urban transportation, ttc
brief: Approving a budget adjustment to buy 105 gasoline-powered Wheel-Trans paratransit buses — 55 six-metre and 50 seven-metre ProMaster buses — for delivery between 2026 and 2029 to replace vehicles reaching the end of their design life, goes to the TTC Board for approval. The adjustment adds $34.931 million to the TTC's 2026-2031 capital cash flow for the buses, with no change to the 2025 capital budget. The purchase would go through Metrolinx's Transit Procurement Initiative, the same competitively-procured process the TTC has used since 2017. A separate pilot of smaller electric Wheel-Trans vehicles, likely sedans or SUVs, would test a better fleet mix; if the electric pilot succeeds, these 105 gasoline buses would be the last non-electric ones bought, with the fleet going zero-emission by 2035.

brief: Chair Jamaal Myers is asking the TTC Board to direct staff to find permanent, visible ways to honour Canada's veterans and TTC employees who are veterans — in vehicles, in stations and elsewhere — and to report back by October 2025. The motion notes the TTC already offers free rides on Warrior's Day and Remembrance Day and halts all vehicles at 11 a.m. on Remembrance Day, but says the contributions of veteran staff and Torontonians who served are not well known. If the Board agrees, staff would develop the recognition options for a later decision.
