brief: This is an appointments item: the Civic Appointments Committee must choose 5 candidates to interview for the Toronto Zoo Board, then recommend one to City Council for appointment. Candidate names are confidential.

title: Selection of Candidates for Interview for the Toronto Public Library Board
topics: candidates, library boards; public library boards
brief: This is an appointments item: the Civic Appointments Committee must choose 4 candidates to interview for the Toronto Public Library Board, then recommend one candidate to City Council for appointment. The names are confidential because they are personal information.

title: 399 Markham Road - Appeal of Property Standards Order - Folder Number 25 136910 PRS 00 IV
topics: by-laws, municipal codes, property standards; bylaws
brief: This is a procedural item: a property owner at 399 Markham Road is appealing a city property standards order. The Property Standards Committee will hear the appeal and decide whether the order stands. No policy change is proposed.

title: 23 Thunder Grove, 215 - Appeal of Property Standards Order - Folder Number 24 235663 PRS 00 IV
topics: by-laws, municipal codes, property standards; bylaws
brief: This is a procedural item: a property owner at 23 Thunder Grove, 215 is appealing a city property standards order. The Property Standards Committee will hear the appeal and decide whether the order stands. No policy change is proposed.

title: 1799 St Clair Avenue West - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment and Draft Plan of Subdivision Applications - Appeal Report
topics: Official Plans, appeals;
brief: The developer of three proposed towers of 30, 40 and 45 storeys at 1799 St. Clair Avenue West appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal after council missed its decision deadline. The project would redesignate the land from employment to mixed use, with a publicly accessible space on the site and the purchase of part of the St. Clair right-of-way to expand the site. Council is asked to send city lawyers to oppose the current proposal while talks continue.

title: 0, 119-125, 160 and 200 Benny Stark Street and 116-122 Turnberry Avenue - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Appeal Report
topics: appeals, official plan amendments, zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The developer of a proposed project on Benny Stark Street and Turnberry Avenue — with three-storey townhouses, three mid-rise buildings of 8 to 10 storeys, four towers of 22 to 46 storeys, new public roads and a city park — appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal after council missed its decision deadline. The lands would be redesignated from employment to mixed-use and parks. Council is asked to send city lawyers to oppose the current proposal while talks continue.

title: 2 Tecumseth Street and 125-133 Niagara Street - Part Lot Control Exemption Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: charges, taxes; levies
brief: The lands at 2 Tecumseth Street and 125-133 Niagara Street would be exempted from Part Lot Control for two years, to allow phased construction and financing of the approved mixed-use development — three mixed-use buildings and two non-residential buildings with homes, offices, shops, affordable housing, a public parkland dedication, a multi-use path and Tecumseth Street improvements. Approval would enact the exemption by-law. City Council makes the final decision.

title: City-Initiated Zoning By-law Amendments - Re-allocating Section 37 funds within Ward 13 - Decision Report - Approval
topics: by-laws, official plan amendments; bylaws
brief: Unspent developer-paid Section 37 funds at several Ward 13 sites — including 587-599 Yonge Street, 454-464 Yonge Street, 45 Charles Street East and 601-613 Yonge Street — could be redirected toward buying and improving community space for community or non-profit use in Ward 13. The by-laws would also add the standard clause allowing unused funds to be reallocated after three years. Approval would amend the zoning by-laws. City Council makes the final decision.

title: Renaming of the Community Garden in Joel Weeks Park
topics: naming, parks; conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland
brief: The community garden in Joel Weeks Park would be renamed 'Carol Sutton Garden', honouring the late abstract artist and longtime volunteer who cared for the park since the early 1980s. Sutton's work appears in major collections including the Smithsonian and the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston. City Council makes the final decision.

title: Parking and Traffic Amendments - Dundas Street West - Findings Report on Pilot Initiative
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, parking machines; pay and display machines; pay-and-display machines, ttc
brief: The temporary parking and traffic changes on Dundas Street West between Spadina Avenue and McCaul Street — introduced in May 2024 to support the 505 Dundas streetcar while the 510 Spadina right-of-way was closed — would be made permanent. The changes removed on-street paid parking during construction, replacing it with no-stopping rules in daytime and no-parking overnight, with commercial and accessible loading areas identified with the Chinatown BIA. Because the TTC runs transit on Dundas Street West, full council approval is required. The item lists costs of $322,000.00 and $6,780.00.

title: 5, 5A, 5B and 9 Leslie Street - City Initiated Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
topics: by-laws, official plan amendments; bylaws
brief: City-owned land at 5, 5A, 5B and 9 Leslie Street, south of the Ashbridges Bay Treatment Plant, would get new land use and zoning permissions to allow new utility and transportation infrastructure and new natural areas. The lands include the Ashbridges Bay Landform, built for erosion and sediment control, with 2.5 hectares for the expansion of Tommy Thompson Park and 1.25 hectares of publicly accessible shoreline. Approval would amend the Official Plan and zoning. City Council makes the final decision.

title: 604 Bay Street (including entrance address 610 Bay Street) - Alterations to and Demolition of Heritage Attributes of a Designated Property under Sections 33 and 34 of the Ontario Heritage Act and Authority to Enter into a Heritage Easement Agreement
topics: demolitions, heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: Alterations and partial demolition of the heritage-designated former Gray Coach Terminal at 604 Bay Street -- completed in 1931 in Art Deco style as one of Canada's first purpose-built motor coach terminals -- go to Council for approval. The work would allow a 16-storey mixed-use building, and the future leaseholder of the City-owned site would enter a heritage easement agreement for long-term protection.

title: Pay-and-Display Parking - Various Streets - June 2025 (Non-Delegated)
topics: parking, parking regulations; parking by-laws; parking bylaws
brief: Changes to paid parking on TTC-served streets in Wards 9 and 14 are proposed — adding new pay-and-display locations and removing some — to encourage parking turnover near businesses. The Toronto Parking Authority and Transportation Services identified the locations together. Because the TTC runs transit on the streets, full council approval is required.

title: Dundas Street West - Accessible Loading Zone
topics: loading zones, parking regulations, traffic regulations; drop off areas; drop off zones; loading spaces; pick up areas; pick up zones, parking by-laws; parking bylaws
brief: A new accessible loading zone is proposed on the north side of Dundas Street West near Pacific Avenue, for Wheel-Trans users and accessible permit holders visiting the Community Junction at 2934 Dundas Street West, operating at all times except 4-6 p.m. weekday afternoons. Staff also found a mismatch between the by-lawed parking rules and posted signs that would be fixed. Because the TTC runs transit on Dundas Street West, full council approval is required. The item lists a $3.00 fee.

title: 604-610 Bay Street and 130 Elizabeth Street - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: official plan amendments, rezoning, zoning bylaws; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: A 16-storey building at 604-610 Bay Street and a 43-storey building at 130 Elizabeth Street are proposed on a City-owned site, with 858 rental homes including 245 affordable units, shops, and a Toronto Paramedic Services facility. The project integrates the designated heritage former Gray Coach Terminal building, completed in 1931 in Art Deco style. Approval would amend the Official Plan and zoning. City Council makes the final decision.

title: Ontario Line - Construction Update - Second Quarter 2025
topics: construction, transportation; building, transportation services
brief: This is a procedural item: the Toronto and East York Community Council is asked to receive a second-quarter 2025 update on Ontario Line construction within its boundaries. The report covers station work, the four main construction packages, Metrolinx's responses to council's recommendations, building condition surveys, truck safety plans and community engagement. No policy change is proposed.

title: Use of Nathan Phillips Square for Various Events - October 1, 2025 - April 30, 2026
topics: arts and culture, festivals and special events; community events; community festivals; cultural events; events; festivals
brief: Event organizers at Nathan Phillips Square from October 1, 2025 to April 30, 2026 would be allowed to operate beer and wine gardens serving alcohol — including VQA wine gardens — subject to provincial approval, the Medical Officer of Health's approval and City conditions. The list includes the Hockey Hall of Fame, Maple Leaf Sports and Entertainment Foundation and the Canadian Olympic Committee. Council approval is required.

title: 1251-1311 Yonge Street - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
brief: Two mixed-use towers of 43 and 47 storeys, with 832 homes, are proposed at 1251-1311 Yonge Street, connected by a 3-storey podium, plus a new 366-square-metre park and about 1,283 square metres of commercial space. The Official Plan change is needed to allow the heights and redesignate part of the property as open space. Approval would amend the Official Plan and zoning. City Council makes the final decision.

title: 15 Glen Morris Street - Alterations to and Demolition of Heritage Attributes of a Designated Property under Sections 33 and 34 of the Ontario Heritage Act and Authority to Enter into a Heritage Easement Agreement
topics: demolitions, heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: Alterations and partial demolition of the heritage-designated Samuel Bennett House at 15 Glen Morris Street -- an 1878 one-and-a-half-storey Ontario house with a verandah and gable dormer -- go to Council for approval. The work would allow an 8-storey residential building behind the kept and rebuilt facades, under a heritage easement agreement.

title: 132, 136, 138, 142, 144 and 148 Dundas Street West and 24 Jefferson Avenue - Inclusion on the Heritage Register
topics: heritage properties, planning; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: Seven properties — at 132, 136, 138, 142, 144 and 148 Dundas Street West and 24 Jefferson Avenue — are up for the City's Heritage Register. The Dundas properties include the 1907 Wineberg Apartments, a 3-storey brick walk-up with street-level shops that reflects the early-20th-century main-street character of what was once 'The Ward'. Listing recognizes their heritage value but does not ban future changes. City Council makes the final decision.

title: 25 Dalhousie Street and 30 Mutual Street - Amendment to Section 37 Agreement to Permit a Seasonal Outdoor Patio
topics: easements, pedestrian walkways; footpaths; pedestrian ways; walking paths; walkways
brief: The Section 37 agreement at 25 Dalhousie Street and 30 Mutual Street would be amended to allow two seasonal outdoor patios — 48 square metres and 46 square metres — in the publicly accessible pedestrian walkway on the site. The walkway was secured as a public access easement in favour of the City. Approval would let the retail units operate the patios under City terms. City Council makes the final decision.

title: 120 Bouchette Street - Application for an Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment - Appeal Report
topics: official plan amendments, rezoning, zoning bylaws; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The developer of a proposed mixed-use project with three towers of 43, 46 and 49 storeys and 1,626 homes at 120 Bouchette Street, in the McCleary District, appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal after council missed its decision deadline. Council is asked to send city lawyers to oppose the current proposal while talks continue and precinct planning is coordinated.

title: 1601-1603 Bathurst Street - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment Applications - Appeal Report
topics: appeals, official plan amendments, zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The developer of a proposed 7-storey, 74-unit rental building at 1601-1603 Bathurst Street appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal after council missed its decision deadline. The proposal would demolish an existing 4-storey rental building with 9 rental units while keeping the 6-storey rental building next door. Council is asked to send city lawyers to oppose the current proposal while talks continue.

title: 640 Sheppard Avenue East - Appeal of Property Standards Order - Folder Number: 25 144979 PRS 00 IV
topics: by-laws, municipal codes, property maintenance, property standards; bylaws, grounds maintenance; groundskeeping
brief: This is a procedural item: a property owner at 640 Sheppard Avenue East is appealing a city property standards order. The Property Standards Committee will hear the appeal and decide whether the order stands. No policy change is proposed.

title: 102 Rajah Street - Appeal of Property Standards Order - Folder Number: 25 140181 PRS 00 IV
topics: by-laws, municipal codes, property maintenance, property standards; bylaws, grounds maintenance; groundskeeping
brief: This is a procedural item: a property owner at 102 Rajah Street is appealing a city property standards order. The Property Standards Committee will hear the appeal and decide whether the order stands. No policy change is proposed.

title: 62 Orchard Park Drive - Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: affordable housing, buildings, rezoning; affordable homes; housing projects, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: City staff recommend approving zoning changes to allow a four-storey building with 47 affordable rental homes at 62 Orchard Park Drive, on a surface parking lot next to West Hill United Church and the MAAT youth centre. A Holding provision would ensure infrastructure matters are addressed. Council would amend the zoning by-law to permit the project. The project was approved for $50,000 in pre-development funding through the city's Open Door program.

title: 3434 Lawrence Avenue East, Zoning By-law Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: mixed use areas, rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: City staff recommend approving zoning changes to allow two L-shaped residential buildings of 10 to 23 storeys at 3434 Lawrence Avenue East, with 855 homes and about 559.5 square metres of ground-floor commercial space. A new north-south public road and a new public park would also be part of the redevelopment. A Holding provision would ensure infrastructure matters are addressed, and council would amend the zoning by-law to permit the project.

title: 672 to 676 Birchmount Road - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment Applications - Decision Report - Approval
topics: development, official plan amendments, residential properties, rezoning; developing land; development (land); land development, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments, residential real estate
brief: City staff recommend approving Official Plan and zoning changes to allow a seven-storey residential building with 226 homes at 672-676 Birchmount Road. The building would total about 18,300 square metres with two levels of underground parking. Council would amend the planning rules to permit the project.

title: Corporate Drive - Accessible Loading Zone
topics: accessibility, loading zones, specialized paratransit services; accessible public transportation; accessible transit; accessible transit service; door to door service; special mobility services; wheel trans; wheel-trans; wheeltrans, barrier-free design; universal design; wheelchair accessible, drop off areas; drop off zones; loading spaces; pick up areas; pick up zones
brief: Transportation staff recommend creating an accessible loading zone operating at all times on the north side of Corporate Drive, east of Consilium Place, to give Wheel-Trans users and accessible permit holders curbside access to the Medical Centre Dialysis Clinic at 78 Corporate Drive. Nearby pay-parking rules would shift to fit it in, with no loss of parking spaces; the existing parking machines charge $3.00 per hour. Because the TTC runs buses on this street, city council approval is required.

title: 2823, 2825, 2827 and 2829 Eglinton Avenue East - Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Approval
topics: zoning, zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: City staff recommend approving zoning changes to allow a 14-storey mixed-use building with 190 homes and ground-floor retail at 2823-2829 Eglinton Avenue East. The building would be 49.3 metres tall with one level of underground parking, accessed from Oswego Road. Council would amend the zoning by-law to permit the project.

title: Review of the Order Paper
brief: This is a procedural item: City Council reviews the order paper, the list of items to be considered at the meeting. No decision is being asked for.

title: Presentations, Introductions and Announcements
brief: This is a procedural item: various presentations, introductions and announcements are made during the meeting. No decisions are being asked for.

title: Petitions
brief: This is a procedural item: members of council may file petitions during the meeting, to be received for the record. No decision is being asked for.

title: Declarations of Interest
brief: This is a procedural item: members of council declare any interests under the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act. No decision is being asked for.

title: Introduction of Committee Reports and New Business from City Officials
brief: This is a procedural item: the mayor and committee chairs introduce committee reports and new business from city officials — including reports from the Executive Committee, Board of Health, Corporations Nominating Panel, Economic and Community Development, General Government, Infrastructure and Environment, and Planning and Housing committees and the four community councils. No decision is being asked for.

title: Confirmation of Minutes
brief: This is a procedural item: City Council will confirm the minutes from its regular meeting held on May 21 and 22, 2025, as an accurate record.

title: Call to Order
brief: This is a procedural item: the council meeting opens with the call to order, O Canada and a moment of silence. No decision is being asked for.

title: Delegation of Authority Update: April 2 - June 1, 2025
body: Toronto Parking Authority - Audit and Risk Management Committee
topics: parking, parking authorities; parking authority
brief: This is a procedural item: the Toronto Parking Authority board is asked to receive for information the update on decisions the President made under delegated authority from April 2 to June 1, 2025. The President can make commitments up to $500,000 (raised from $250,000 in 2021) and award non-competitive contracts up to $250,000. No policy change is proposed.

title: Toronto Parking Authority - State of Good Repair Program
body: Toronto Parking Authority - Audit and Risk Management Committee
topics: maintenance, parking, repairs;
brief: City staff and the TTC would prepare a business case for repairing the parking garages at City Hall (Car Park 36) and 40 York Street (Car Park 52), for the 2026 budget process, if the Toronto Parking Authority board agrees. A 2021 building condition assessment found an estimated $280 million (in 2024 dollars) backlog of rehabilitation and critical repairs across the authority's garages. The report also references figures of $20.17 million, $15.38 million, $12.6 million, $128 million and $152 million.

title: Toronto Parking Authority Enterprise Risk Management
body: Toronto Parking Authority - Audit and Risk Management Committee
topics: parking;
brief: Approval of the refreshed 2025 Enterprise Risk Management report — developed with the board over several months — setting out how the authority identifies and manages its major risks is before the Toronto Parking Authority board. The report follows a five-step risk management process.

title: Toronto Parking Authority - 2025 May 31 Year-to-Date Financial Performance (First Five Months Results)
body: Toronto Parking Authority - Audit and Risk Management Committee
brief: This is a procedural item: the Toronto Parking Authority board is asked to receive for information its financial results for the first five months of 2025. Net income was $18.1 million (+$2.4 million versus plan); revenue was $69.2 million (-$1.0 million versus plan, +$4.3 million versus 2024); operating costs were $46.3 million; finance income was $1.4 million; amortization was $1.1 million lower than plan. The authority invested $5.6 million in capital projects, on track for a full-year capital plan of $55.6 million, supported by $25.8 million in city funding for Bike Share and EV initiatives. The report also references figures of $44 million, $47 million, $2 million and $5 million. No policy change is proposed.

title: Advancing Housing Sites: Supporting Housing Construction on Public Land at 267-275 Merton Street, and 610 Bay Street and 130 Elizabeth Street
topics: planning, supportive housing; alternative housing; special needs housing; supported housing
brief: Two city-owned rental projects — 267-275 Merton Street and 610 Bay Street/130 Elizabeth Street, together over 1,350 rental homes including at least 369 affordable — are at risk of stalling as market rents fall and project costs rise. Council decides on staff instructions to keep both projects viable and on asking Ottawa and CMHC to fast-track construction funding. These are among the city's signature projects for getting purpose-built and affordable rental construction started in 2025.

title: Housing Action Plan: Avenues Policy Review - Phase Two Work Plan
topics: Avenues, housing, mid rise buildings; arterial corridors; main streets, homes; residences
brief: Toronto's main streets are headed for a major round of mid-rise housing zoning work. Council is asked to adopt a phase two work plan that will develop as-of-right zoning for mid-rise buildings along Avenues, with a multi-stage public consultation process across the city. Phase one already updated the Official Plan vision for Avenues through OPA 778, adopted in February 2025.

title: Housing Action Plan: Incorporating Low-rise Residential Lands into Zoning By-law 569-2013 - North York District - Final Report
topics: housing, low rise buildings, zoning, zoning bylaws; homes; residences, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: About 323 North York properties left out of the city-wide zoning by-law since 2012 would finally come under Zoning By-law 569-2013, with standards consistent with the former municipal rules and the Official Plan. Council decides whether to adopt the zoning amendments. The change lets these lots use city-wide rules such as the removal of parking minimums and new missing middle housing permissions, supporting the Housing Action Plan target of 285,000 homes over ten years.

title: Housing Accelerator Fund: Apartment Infill Study - Residential Infill Report
topics: apartments, infill development; infill housing; infilling; residential infill
brief: Infill housing on existing apartment sites would get a simpler, faster approval path under the Apartment Infill Study. Council is being asked to change zoning rules and develop new tools and best practices to streamline apartment infill proposals, including purpose-built rental housing. The study aims at contextually appropriate additions to the city's apartment neighbourhoods to address current housing needs. The item's source material also references $471.1 million.

title: Housing Accelerator Fund: Expanding Permissions in Neighbourhoods for Low-Rise Sixplexes - Final Report
topics: [activities in planning and development], affordable housing, multi-unit dwellings; affordable homes; housing projects, multi residential apartment buildings; multi residential buildings; multi unit buildings; multi unit dwellings; multi-residential apartment buildings; multi-residential buildings; multi-unit buildings; multi-unit residential buildings; residential multi unit dwellings; residential multi-unit dwellings
brief: Council votes on amending the Official Plan and zoning rules to allow them, using federal Housing Accelerator Fund support to add more gentle-density housing. The city's Housing Accelerator Fund agreement with CMHC is worth $471.1 million (signed December 2023, with $235.6 million received so far), and this item fulfills the city's commitment under that agreement to allow more low-rise multi-unit housing. With at least 830,000 new Torontonians expected by 2051, the change would shape how growth reaches low-rise streets, where new housing has so far been mostly mid- and high-rise apartments.

title: Expanding Housing Options in Neighbourhoods - Multiplex - Monitoring Program - Final Report
topics: high rise buildings, housing; homes; residences, tall buildings
brief: City-wide zoning rules for multiplexes are back before Council after a monitoring program's final report. Council is being asked to approve zoning changes for this low-rise housing type, updating how multiplexes fit into the land-development section of the city's rulebook. With at least 830,000 new Torontonians expected by 2051, the changes shape how neighbourhoods can absorb growth at the same scale as their streets today.

title: Property Included on the City's Heritage Register - Consideration of Objection for 1751 Bayview Avenue
topics: culture (sc), heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties
brief: The 1930s apartment building at 1751 Bayview Avenue, on the east side of Bayview Avenue between Eglinton Avenue East and Parkhurst Boulevard in Leaside-Bennington, would stay on the city's Heritage Register. Council is being asked to reject the property owner's objection to the listing under the Ontario Heritage Act. The decision keeps the building flagged for its heritage value.

title: 2025 Toronto Heritage Grant Awards
topics: heritage conservation districts, restoration, subsidies and grants; financial assistance; financial incentives; financial subsidy; grant and subsidy programs; grant programs; grants; grants programs; incentives; subsidies; subsidy and grant programs, heritage districts; historic areas, rehabilitation (property)
brief: Twenty-two heritage grants totalling $317,000.00 are up for approval under the Toronto Heritage Grant Program. Council is being asked to approve the grants, which are expected to generate about $660,225.61 in private investment for conservation work on heritage properties across the city. Owners of house form buildings can receive up to $10,000.00, or up to $20,000.00 every ten years for replacing an entire cedar or slate roof; the program itself has a budget of $317,000.00.

title: 36 Green Valley Road - Inclusion on the Heritage Register
topics: heritage designation, neighbourhoods, property (sc); cultural neighbourhoods; ethnic neighbourhoods; neighborhoods
brief: The property at 36 Green Valley Road, in the Bridle Path-Sunnybrook-York Mills neighbourhood, is recommended for the city's Heritage Register for its cultural heritage value. Listing would flag the property as historically significant and require the owner to give the city notice before any demolition. City Council makes the final call on listings.

title: 5576 Yonge Street - Official Plan Amendment, Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Refusal
topics: buildings, official plan amendments, rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend refusing a proposal for two mixed-use buildings, 35 and 25 storeys with 608 homes and street-level shops, at 5576 Yonge Street. One issue staff flag is that the plan would require moving an existing city sanitary sewer that runs through the middle of the site. North York Community Council is being asked to adopt the refusal.

title: 234 Sheppard Avenue West and 223 Harlandale Avenue - Official Plan Amendment, Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Appeal
topics: buildings, official plan amendments, rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Staff recommend refusing a proposal at 234 Sheppard Avenue West and 223 Harlandale Avenue: a four-storey, 15-unit condo facing Harlandale and an 11-storey mixed-use building with 43 rental homes and street-level shops facing Sheppard. North York Community Council is being asked to adopt the refusal, keeping the current rules for the site. If the applicant appeals, city staff would defend the refusal at the Ontario Land Tribunal.

title: 690-720 Sheppard Avenue East Official Plan Amendment and Zoning By-law Amendment Applications - Appeal Report
topics: applications, official plan amendments, rezoning; application process, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Two mixed-use buildings, 32 and 28 storeys with 705 homes on eight-storey podiums, are proposed at 690-720 Sheppard Avenue East. The applicant appealed the planning applications to the Ontario Land Tribunal, and North York Community Council is being asked to direct the City Solicitor to oppose the appeal at the hearing.

title: 1350 Sheppard Avenue West - Zoning Amendment Application - Decision Report - Approval
topics: by-laws, housing, zoning bylaws; bylaws, homes; residences, zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: The applicant behind the William Baker / Arbo District Phase 1 project at 1350 Sheppard Avenue West wants to amend the site's zoning by-law: the unit count would rise from 1,400 to 1,700, and the minimum sizes for two- and three-bedroom units would shrink. City Council is being asked to approve the amendment, which sets what can be built on the site. The item's source material also references $5,000,000.00.

title: Amendments to Chapter 918 as it Relates to Applications within Ward 15
topics: municipal codes, neighbourhoods, on-street parking, parking, parking pads, residential properties; boulevard parking; front yard parking; off street parking; off street permit parking, cultural neighbourhoods; ethnic neighbourhoods; neighborhoods, curb parking; curbside parking; street parking, residential real estate
brief: Residents in parts of Ward 15 (the former Wards 22 and 25) who apply for front-yard parking are being turned down solely because on-street permit parking exists on their street, even where a parking pad would otherwise be allowed. The proposed change to Chapter 918 would stop that automatic refusal so each application is judged on its own merits. North York Community Council is being asked to approve the change.

title: Garratt Boulevard - Heavy Truck Prohibition
topics: community & life (sc), community safety, heavy trucks, traffic; motor vehicle traffic; motorized traffic; traffic conditions; traffic flow; trip info; tripinfo
brief: Heavy trucks would be banned from Garratt Boulevard, between Wilson Avenue and Gilley Road. The motion is meant to keep two-way traffic safe as construction traffic grows with development of the Downsview lands north of Ancaster; affected trucks would instead use Dufferin Street, Beffort Road and Hanover Road. Council is being asked to approve the prohibition.

title: 911X Castlefield Avenue - Request to Demolish the Non-Residential Building
topics: buildings, demolitions, residential properties; residential real estate
brief: The owner of 911X Castlefield Avenue has applied to demolish the non-residential building on the property. Under the former City of York's demolition rules, City Council itself must decide: it can grant the permit, grant it with conditions, or refuse it.

title: 2255 Sheppard Avenue East - Inclusion on the Heritage Register
topics: official plan amendments, property (sc), rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: The property at 2255 Sheppard Avenue East, on the south side of Sheppard between Consumers Road and Victoria Park Avenue in the Henry Farm neighbourhood, is recommended for the city's Heritage Register for its cultural heritage value. Listing would flag the property as historically significant and require the owner to give the city notice before any demolition. City Council makes the final call on listings.

title: Maniza Road - Parking Restrictions
topics: parking prohibitions; no parking
brief: Parking rules near St. Norbert Catholic School would tighten during school hours. City Council is asked to rescind the existing 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday to Friday prohibition on the east side of Maniza Road between Spalding Road and Plewes Road, and instead prohibit parking from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., Monday to Friday, from September 1 to June 30, on the east side of Maniza Road between Katherine Road and Plewes Road — no parking rather than no stopping, since parents need to stop briefly for drop-off. Drivers near the school would be affected.

title: Appointment of Public Members to the Waterfront Toronto Board
topics: appointments, public appointments;
brief: This is a procedural item: the Corporations Nominating Panel would recommend three public members to City Council for appointment to the Waterfront Toronto Board, for terms ending June 27, 2028. Confidential attachments would stay confidential. No policy change is proposed.

title: Appointment of Public Member to the Toronto Hydro Board
topics: appointments, public appointments;
brief: This is a procedural item: the Corporations Nominating Panel would recommend two public members to City Council for appointment to the Toronto Hydro Board, for terms ending June 27, 2027. Confidential attachments on the candidates would stay confidential. No policy change is proposed.

title: Waiving of Toronto Parking Authority Fees on Bond Street - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
topics: parking fees; parking charges; parking rates
brief: The Toronto Parking Authority would be asked to waive $115,230 in fees tied to the permanent removal of three paid parking spaces and the relocation of two parking machines for the St. Michael's Hospital redevelopment on Bond Street. Council would make the request in connection with the hospital's new 6-storey Shuter Wing addition and public realm improvements on Shuter and Bond streets, which the hospital values at close to $1.5 million. The hospital, a downtown teaching and trauma centre with over one million patient visits a year, provided the improvements at the urging of the local BIA and former ward councillor. The fee waiver would offset the revenue the parking authority loses from the removed spaces.

title: East Mall Bus 111 Route Public Consultation - by Councillor Stephen Holyday, seconded by Councillor Vincent Crisanti
topics: bus routes;
brief: The TTC would be asked to pause its rerouting of the 111 East Mall bus and four new bus pads on Beaver Bend Crescent until residents and the local school are consulted. Council would ask the TTC to hold off on permanently moving the southbound 111 off The East Mall and into the West Deane Park residential neighbourhood — a change made because three existing stops did not meet new accessibility standards — after residents were surprised by tree-protection hoarding in late May 2025 with no prior consultation. The new route would run down narrow streets through the pick-up and drop-off area of Josyf Cardinal Slipyj elementary school. Riders of the 45-year-old route, residents and the school community would be affected.

title: Review of Seasonal Grass Cutting and Inter-Divisional Coordination - by Councillor Shelley Carroll, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: maintenance;
brief: Grass cutting could start earlier in April and be better coordinated across City divisions. Council would have staff report back through the 2026 budget process on adding an earlier April cut — right-of-way mowing now starts in late May, by which time weeds like dandelions have gone to seed — and on coordinating mowing and groundskeeping schedules across divisions so parks, boulevards, libraries and community centres are not maintained on mismatched schedules. The motion responds to rising spring complaints about overgrown weeds and patchy maintenance. Residents would see more consistent-looking public spaces.

title: Green P Parking Lot Usage Data - by Councillor Paul Ainslie, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
topics: land use, parking, transportation (sc);
brief: Green P parking lot usage data would be published on the City's open data portal with quarterly updates. Council would request that the Toronto Parking Authority release the dataset to support data-driven decisions, after the motion argued the City is making major real estate decisions without comprehensive parking data. The stated aims are better real estate planning, transportation management and identification of underused or overused parking assets, particularly in intensifying areas. Planners, developers and residents tracking land use would use the data.

title: Construction Project 25ECS-RD-104LR: Removal of Sidewalk Installation in Brookhaven Neighbourhood - by Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Vincent Crisanti
topics: construction, sidewalks; building
brief: Planned new sidewalks on four Brookhaven streets would be dropped from a fall 2025 road resurfacing contract after residents voted overwhelmingly against them. Council would amend construction project 25ECS-RD-104LR to remove sidewalk installation on Noranda Drive, Monarchdale Avenue, Westchester Road and Parkchester Road, while proceeding with road resurfacing and other work. The ward councillor held an in-person meeting on June 10, 2025, where 72 residents attended and a show-of-hands vote came out 1 in favour and 71 opposed. The change affects pedestrians and homeowners on those streets, who would keep the current no-sidewalk layout.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Heritage Toronto for Heritage Plaque at 101 Dewson Street - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: conservation, heritage preservation, historic sites, plaques; environmental conservation; environmental improvements; environmental management; environmental protection; environmental stewardship; greening, heritage buildings; heritage sites; historical sites, heritage plaques; heritage toronto plaques; historic markers; historic plaques; historical markers; local markers; provincial plaques, historic preservation; historical preservation
brief: A heritage plaque at 101 Dewson Street would mark the house's role as a hub of Black, gay and lesbian activism in 1980s Toronto. Council would release $10,000 in Section 37 developer community benefits to Heritage Toronto for the plaque at the Dufferin Grove home of writer and activist Makeda Silvera, where she and Stephanie Martin started the Dewson House Collective in 1983 and where groups including Lesbians of Colour, Sister Vision Press and Zami were born. The motion recounts the house's links to the Black Women's Collective, Black Coalition for AIDS Prevention and Blockorama. The plaque would give passersby a permanent record of the site's history.

title: Waterfront School Playground Expansion - Amendment to existing nominal lease and ancillary real estate agreements with Toronto District School Board - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Amber Morley
topics: schools; community use of schools; educational institutions; school cafeterias; school classrooms; school gymnasiums
brief: The Waterfront School playground at 627-635 Queens Quay West would grow by about 260 square metres under an expanded lease with the Toronto District School Board. Council would amend the City's existing nominal lease, licence and shared-use agreements — dating to the 1997 joint construction of the school, community centre, childcare centre and play space — to add the land for the playground master plan. The City-funded scope covers the south turf field with a new running path, sand jumping pit, goal posts, baseball backstop, storage shed and tree planting, building on 2024's Section 37 allocation. Students and neighbourhood families would share the improved play space.

title: Request to Accept In-Kind Community Benefits for 49 Ontario Street Rental Housing Development - by Councillor Chris Moise, seconded by Mayor Olivia Chow
topics: community benefits, rental housing; rental properties; rental units
brief: The City would accept land instead of cash as the community benefit tied to the rental housing development at 49 Ontario Street. Council would accept the developer's offer of in-kind land for the city in place of a cash payment, connected to the site plan for three buildings of 9, 45 and 49 storeys with 1,226 rental units (including about 246 affordable units), retail, office, heritage rowhouses and a 581-square-metre public park along Berkeley Street. The owner converted the project to full rental tenure and applied through the City's Rental Housing Supply Program and Purpose-Built Rental Incentives Stream. The decision affects what the public gets in exchange for the development's density.

title: Action to Address Speed Racing on Expressways - by Councillor Jon Burnside, seconded by Councillor Shelley Carroll
topics: races, traffic speed; marathons; runs; walkathons
brief: Overnight speed racing on expressways like the Don Valley Parkway could face joint action by police and the City. Council would request that the Toronto Police Service Board ask the Chief of Police to consider collaborative enforcement on speed racing on expressways and nearby streets, and to include the parkway in noise enforcement and education work, after a rise in complaints about loud overnight vehicle noise along the Don Valley Parkway and Highway 404 corridor. Council took similar action in 2020 and 2021. Residents near the expressways dealing with the noise and safety impacts are the ones affected.

title: Targeted Lane Re-Openings to Reduce Congestion During Construction Downtime - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: congestion, construction; building, gridlock
brief: Construction contractors could be required to reopen traffic lanes on nearby routes during major events and on evenings and weekends when no work is happening. Council would direct staff to assess the feasibility, project by project, of temporarily reopening lanes on parallel routes during heavy-disruption periods, building on the Strategic Capital Coordination Office, the 2023-2026 Congestion Management Plan and the Enhancing Capital Construction Delivery program. The motion responds to growing congestion as infrastructure investment overlaps with special events and peak travel. Drivers and transit riders navigating construction zones would feel the difference.

title: Open or Closed? Improving Public Information on Pool Closures and Alerts - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: outdoor pools; outdoor swimming pools
brief: Swimmers would get accurate, easy-to-find pool closure information online under this motion. Council would direct parks staff to keep the Pool & Water Play Closures & Service Alerts webpage accurate and current, and to review how easy the information is to find and use — after residents showed up at closed pools during the recent heat wave, found the webpage outdated, and learned 311 did not have the closure details. Pools, wading areas, splash pads and recreation centres are part of the City's Heat Relief Network. Anyone heading out to cool off on a hot day would benefit from reliable closure alerts.

title: Preserving Community Access at Loretto College School - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: catholic schools;
brief: Public access to the field and green space at Loretto College School in Davenport could be preserved through a formal shared-use agreement with the Toronto Catholic District School Board. Council would direct parks staff to approach the Board after its field renewal project — which would remove a City-operated wading pool and fence the field's perimeter — raised concerns from neighbours, including a petition with over 1,000 signatures. The field has been shared informally for decades but never had a formal agreement, and the ward has a defined parkland need. Local residents who use the space to meet, gather and play would be the ones affected.

title: Results of Interest Arbitration Between the City of Toronto and Toronto Civic Employees Union Local 416 - Paramedics - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: arbitration, paramedics, unions; adjudication, labour unions; trade unions
brief: Toronto's paramedics would get their new contract terms under an arbitrator's June 23, 2025 award, and Council must act to put them in place. Council would authorize budget adjustments to the 2025 Non-Program expenditure and Toronto Paramedic Service operating budgets, and changes to pay rates, benefits and related items, reflecting the interest arbitration award for the Toronto Civic Employees Union Local 416 paramedics unit. Because the award came from interest arbitration, neither side ratifies it; Council direction is required to begin implementation. The motion is urgent because the award arrived after the council agenda closed.

title: Re-Opening and Amending Item 2025.CC30.8 - 943 - 963 Eglinton Avenue East and 23 Brentcliffe Road - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Josh Matlow
topics: planning tribunals; omb; ontario municipal board
brief: This is a procedural item: Council is asked to correct the address of an off-site parkland dedication in its earlier decision on the 943-963 Eglinton Avenue East and 23 Brentcliffe Road development, changing 161 Vanderhoof Avenue to the correct 131 Vanderhoof Avenue, adjacent to Leonard Linton Park. The correction follows Council's May 2025 adoption of a settlement offer and directions for the Ontario Land Tribunal hearing. A pre-condition to the Tribunal's order, tied to the applicant's outstanding appeal of Official Plan Amendment 450 (Laird in Focus), was also inadvertently omitted. No policy change is involved.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 and Section 42 Funds to Amend the 2025 Capital Budget and 2026-2034 Plan for Parks and Recreation for Canoe Landing Off Leash Area Improvements in Ward 10 - by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: funding, parks; conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland, financing
brief: Dog owners using Canoe Landing Park would get a redesigned permanent off-leash area under a $1.69 million project funded by developer money. Council would amend the Parks and Recreation capital budget to create the Canoe Landing Park Off Leash Area Improvements project, with $0.1 million in 2025 and $1.59 million in 2026, drawing $795,000 from Section 37 benefits collected at 400-420 King Street West and another $795,000 from Section 42 cash-in-lieu from the 8 and 30 Widmer Street development. Public engagement runs summer to fall 2025, with construction expected in 2026. The existing off-leash area no longer meets community needs, so the redesign would affect local dog owners and park users in Ward 10.

title: Addressing Gaps in the City’s Heat Relief Strategy - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Alejandra Bravo
topics: climate, environment (sc), extreme heat alerts, health (sc), public health, temperature; heat
brief: The City's Heat Relief Strategy would get a formal review plus immediate upgrades ahead of the next heat warning. Council would direct staff to review the strategy and pursue changes — such as longer pool hours, surge shelter spaces and cooling measures — after a summer that saw the humidex hit 46, health rules close some pools, and Project Water unable to deliver water bottles to people experiencing homelessness for the first time in 25 years. Ahead of the June 22 heat event, the Mayor's office deployed three water trucks running 24/7 and 14,000 bottles of water through outreach workers, with Red Cross volunteers checking on seniors and low-income residents. People without air conditioning, seniors and those experiencing homelessness are most at risk in extreme heat. Council would also direct up to $50,000 from the corporate extreme weather reserve to Project FoodChain so frontline agencies can distribute at least 500,000 bottles of water in 2025.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds to Uptown Yonge Business Improvement Area for Seating and Streetscape Improvements - by Councillor Mike Colle, seconded by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin
topics: benches (street furniture), business improvement areas, urban form; bia; business improvement associations, streetscapes; urban landscape
brief: Twenty-two new benches would go up on the west side of Yonge Street between Glengrove Avenue West and Erskine Avenue for $63,000. Council would forward $63,000 in Section 37 funds from the development at 2360-2376 Yonge Street to the UPtown Yonge Business Improvement Area as the 50 percent contribution the City matches for the streetscape program, on signing of a funding agreement. The BIA installed benches on the east side of Yonge in 2024. Pedestrians and shoppers along the corridor would get the new seating.

title: Authorization to Release Section 37 Funds for the Pelham Park Hub - Giving Youth Leaders of Tomorrow a Brighter Today - by Councillor Alejandra Bravo, seconded by Councillor Gord Perks
topics: youth programs; leadership programs
brief: A new youth hub at 61 Pelham Park Gardens would get $10,000 toward its renovation into a space for mentorship, leadership, digital literacy and recreation programs. Council would add $10,000 gross ($0 net) to the 2025 Non-Program operating budget, funded by Section 37 developer community benefits, for capital work including painting, flooring, window replacement, washroom upgrades and new doors and locks. Toronto Community Housing Corporation would run the Youth Leaders of Tomorrow Hub, developed with tenant leaders, youth and the Toronto Police Service. Young people in Pelham Park and surrounding Toronto Community Housing communities are the intended users.

title: Fixing Roads Faster - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: road maintenance, roads; circles (roads); circuits (roads); courts (roads); crescents (roads); drives (roads); gardens (roads); gates (roads); groves (roads); heights (roads); roadways; squares (roads); streets; terraces (roads); trails (roads), roads maintenance; sidewalk maintenance; sidewalks maintenance; summer maintenance; winter maintenance
brief: Toronto would accelerate permanent repaving of its worst pothole-ridden roads, aiming to finish this construction season's priority list by the fourth quarter of 2025. Council would direct Transportation Services to identify the roads in the worst condition and repave — not just patch — them, using $350 million in additional provincial funding secured through the new deal for roads and public infrastructure. The City has filled over 154,000 potholes so far in 2025 after 285,000 last year. Drivers, cyclists and transit riders across the city would use the repaired roads.

title: Re-Opening King Street for Business: Keeping Toronto’s Downtown Core and Canada’s Financial District Moving - by Councillor Brad Bradford, seconded by Councillor Stephen Holyday
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, congestion, public transit, transportation; gridlock, local transit; mass transit; public transport; public transportation; surface transit; transit; transit services; urban transportation, transportation services, ttc
brief: King Street between Spadina Avenue and Church Street would reopen to cars while the King and Church intersection stays closed for watermain and streetcar track reconstruction. Council is asked to approve the reopening even as the intersection — closed June 2 to replace a 142-year-old watermain and rebuild TTC tracks, four weeks ahead of schedule, through at least mid-August — remains shut. The motion describes gridlock on the remaining east-west routes from three diverted streetcar lines and concurrent downtown construction, and says Canada's financial district must stay accessible. Drivers and transit riders downtown would feel the change.

title: Speeding Up Streetcars: Traffic Amendments on Adelaide Street, King Street and York Street - by Mayor Olivia Chow, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
topics: streetcars, traffic, traffic speed; motor vehicle traffic; motorized traffic; traffic conditions; traffic flow; trip info; tripinfo, street-cars
brief: Temporary parking and traffic changes on Adelaide, King and York streets would keep the 504 King streetcar moving while King and Church is under construction. Council would approve the measures starting July 2, 2025 until streetcar service returns to King and Church: loading zones move from Adelaide Street West to York Street and King Street West, marshalled by traffic control persons, and stopping would be prohibited on Adelaide Street West from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. daily. The changes were agreed with the TTC, Transportation Services and the Financial District BIA. Downtown transit riders and delivery drivers are the most affected. Council would also increase the purchase order with Midome Construction Services for the King and Church streetcar track work by $350,000 — from $3,078,800 to up to $3,428,800 — to pay for additional paid duty officers at seven locations near the worksite to manage traffic.

title: Implementation of Permit Parking on Dundas Street West (Permit Area 1F), Bloor Street West and Quebec Avenue (Permit Area 1B) - by Councillor Gord Perks, seconded by Deputy Mayor Ausma Malik
topics: permit parking; on-street permit parking; parking permits
brief: New developments on Dundas Street West, Bloor Street West and Quebec Avenue could be barred from the local on-street permit parking system. Council would ask Transportation Services to study the feasibility of excluding the developments at 3239-3251 Dundas Street West (Permit Area 1F) and 1930-1938 Bloor Street West plus 3, 5 and 21 Quebec Avenue (Permit Area 1B) from permit parking under Municipal Code Chapter 925, and report back. A public notice would allow deputations at a future Toronto and East York Community Council meeting. The change would affect residents, visitors and tradespeople at those addresses.

title: Accepting a Donation from East York Foundation at Leaside Gardens Memorial Arena - by Councillor Rachel Chernos Lin, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
topics: arenas, donation; bequest; toy drive, indoor hockey rinks; rinks
brief: New scoreboards at Leaside Gardens Memorial Arena would be paid for with a $319,000 donation from the East York Foundation's Dr. Tom Pashby Sport Safety Fund. Council would authorize Parks and Recreation to accept the donation and amend the 2025 capital budget, offsetting the need for City capital funding on this part of the arena work. The upgraded scoreboards would improve the arena experience for local sports leagues and community programming at no net cost to the City. The project would be delivered by the Parks and Recreation capital projects team.

title: Recognition of 50th Anniversary of the Cabbagetown Group Softball League - by Councillor Paula Fletcher, seconded by Councillor Chris Moise
topics: recreation & tourism (sc), sports, sports clubs; badminton clubs; baseball associations; baseball leagues; bowling clubs; cross-country ski clubs; curling clubs; gymnastic clubs; hockey associations; hockey leagues; karate clubs; lacrosse clubs; lawn bowling clubs; ride clubs; rifle clubs; slo-pitch leagues; soccer clubs; soccer leagues; softball associations; softball leagues; swim clubs; tennis clubs; volleyball clubs
brief: This is a recognition item: Council would congratulate the Cabbagetown Group Softball League on its 50th anniversary. The league began 50 years ago as a place for the gay community to play softball, and the motion recounts how it adopted its name to secure City field permits at a time when an openly gay league could not. It is now one of the founding members of the North American Gay Amateur Athletic Association's network of 50-plus leagues. No policy or spending change is proposed.

title: Amending Item 2022.NY29.1 - 824 Sheppard Avenue West, 177, 179 and 181 Cocksfield Avenue- Official Plan Amendment, Zoning Amendment and Rental Housing Demolition and Conversion Application - Final Report - by Councillor James Pasternak, seconded by Councillor Anthony Perruzza
topics: rental housing; rental properties; rental units
brief: The developer of 824 Sheppard Avenue West could demolish 15 vacant rental units sooner, without waiting for excavation and shoring permits. Council would amend its 2022 approval (2022.NY29.1) by deleting the precondition tying demolition permits to the issuance of those permits, letting planning staff issue preliminary demolition approval earlier. The tenants have moved out with assistance and compensation, and Development Review staff support the change, which the motion says would speed up construction and shorten the displacement period. The addresses also include 177, 179 and 181 Cocksfield Avenue.

title: Supporting the North York Harvest Food Bank in meeting rising food scarcity needs in Toronto - by Councillor James Pasternak, seconded by Councillor Lily Cheng
topics: food banks; foodshare
brief: North York Harvest Food Bank's move to a larger warehouse and skills training centre at 4050 Chesswood Drive could get City backing. Council would direct the City Manager to report by the third quarter of 2025 on support options — such as a one-time grant or low-interest loan — for the food bank's capital needs. The motion says food bank visits have tripled amid Toronto's food insecurity emergency and the current warehouse cannot keep up; the new site would double warehousing capacity and add job training and work placements. Northern Toronto residents relying on the food bank, and job seekers using the training centre, would be the beneficiaries.

title: Authorization to Release Sections 37 and 45 Funds to Support Toronto Community Housing Capital Projects at 90 Mornelle Court - by Councillor Paul Ainslie, seconded by Councillor Nick Mantas
topics: funding, social housing; community housing; housing allowance; housing projects; low income housing; non profit housing; non-profit housing; public housing; rent geared to income assistance; rent geared to income housing; rent subsidies; rent supplement; subsidized housing; subsidized rent; subsidized units, financing
brief: Toronto Community Housing residents at 90 Mornelle Court would get a new playground, a renovated basketball court and a seated gathering place for $623,310.07. Council would add $623,310.07 gross ($0 net) to the 2025 Non-Program operating budget, funded by $402,500.00 in Section 37 and $220,810.07 in Section 45 benefits from the 3070 Ellesmere Road development, and forward the money to Toronto Community Housing on signing of a funding agreement. Design and procurement are slated for 2025 with construction in 2026, and Toronto Community Housing would cover any cost overruns. The projects were chosen through consultation with residents and Toronto Community Housing.

title: New Etobicoke Centre Shelter Public Consultation - by Councillor Stephen Holyday, seconded by Councillor Vincent Crisanti
topics: homelessness, persons who are homeless; homeless; homeless individuals
brief: The planned new homeless shelter in Ward 2, Etobicoke Centre, would be paused while the community is consulted. Council would direct staff to halt the real estate transaction, make the shelter's location and details public, and report back by the end of 2025 on a revised public consultation model for shelter sites. The motion follows the ward councillor's account that staff treated the location as confidential and moved to close the deal after he asked for a pause. Residents of Etobicoke Centre would get details and a say before the City commits to the site.

title: 36 Romeo Street - Request for the City Solicitor to Attend at the Toronto Local Appeal Body - by Councillor Frances Nunziata, seconded by Councillor Paula Fletcher
topics: appeals;
brief: The City would defend the Committee of Adjustment's refusal to sever 36 Romeo Street into two lots at the Toronto Local Appeal Body. Council would authorize the City Solicitor to oppose the applicant's appeal of the April 17, 2025 refusal of the severance and variances — covering frontage, lot area, coverage, floor space index, setbacks, storeys, wall height and driveway width — for two new homes. The motion also allows hiring an outside consultant and negotiating a settlement. The appeal's outcome decides whether the two-lot plan proceeds.

title: TransformTO Net Zero Strategy - 2024 Annual Report on Implementation Progress
topics: city initiatives, environmental plans, greenhouse effect; city council priorities; corporate campaigns; council priorities; municipal initiatives, environment plans, greenhouse gas emissions
brief: This is a procedural item: City Council is receiving the 2024 annual progress report for information on the TransformTO Net Zero Strategy, which aims for net zero community-wide emissions by 2040. The report tracks implementation of the 2022–2025 short-term plan; the City directly controls about five per cent of community-wide emissions.

title: F.G. Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway Closure - Bike for Brain Health 2026
topics: highways, races, transportation; freeways; motorways; parkways, marathons; runs; walkathons, transportation services
brief: Up for approval at City Council: closing the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway on Sunday, May 31, 2026, from 2:00 a. m. to 4:00 p.m., for the Bike for Brain Health charity ride supporting the Baycrest Foundation. The start and finish move to the Aga Khan Museum this year because of FIFA World Cup preparations at Exhibition Place. Approval is for one year only, given the provincial review of the Gardiner and DVP upload.

title: Temporary Street Closure for Eastbound F.G. Gardiner Expressway and Northbound Don Valley Parkway - 2026 Toronto Triathlon Festival
topics: highways, major arterial roads, races; freeways; motorways; parkways, marathons; runs; walkathons
brief: Whether to approve closing the eastbound Gardiner Expressway and northbound Don Valley Parkway lanes on Sunday, July 26, 2026, from 2:00 a is before City Council. m. to 12:00 p.m., for the Toronto Triathlon Festival, and to limit other road closures that day within the area bounded by Highway 401, Warden Avenue, Lake Ontario, the Humber River, Queen Street/The Queensway, and Yonge Street to handle overflow traffic. Approval is for one year only, given the provincial review of the Gardiner and DVP upload.

title: Authorized Vehicles in City Parks - Review of Operating Procedures and Policies
topics: city vehicles, parks vehicles, policies and procedures; city owned vehicles; city-owned vehicles; corporate fleet, guidelines; policies, park vehicles
brief: On the agenda at City Council: having staff update the standard terms for permits and contracts that allow vehicles in parks, and to run a public education campaign on authorized vehicle use in parks, how to report problems, and how park assets are protected. The report reviews City policies on vehicle use in parks — limited to trained emergency and service drivers plus permitted third parties — and updates progress on alternative vehicles and a parks electrification pilot.

title: Updates on Vision Zero Road Safety Initiatives: Improving Crossings for Pedestrians, Updated Road Classification Criteria and Other Matters
topics: pedestrians, road safety, traffic control systems; pedestrianization, traffic signal control systems; traffic signal equipment
brief: Up for adoption at City Council: updated road safety policies on pedestrian crossings, crosswalk markings, stop signs, and traffic signals under the Vision Zero plan. The report recommends thirteen new traffic control signals to improve pedestrian crossing protection, one of which would be built as part of adjacent development. The updates follow nine years of the Vision Zero Road Safety Plan and target pedestrian safety as the top priority. The 2025 Vision Zero budget is $99.1 million — $31.7 million in capital and $67.4 million in operating — the largest annual budget for the plan since it began in 2016. The item also continues $3.0 million for expanding the Active and Safe Routes to School program, including $320,000 a year for three years to the Toronto District and Toronto Catholic District school boards.

title: A Strategic Parking Framework for the City of Toronto
topics: city initiatives, parking, transportation; city council priorities; corporate campaigns; council priorities; municipal initiatives, transportation services
brief: Up for approval at City Council: a Strategic Parking Framework to guide citywide parking decisions, and to study whether management of some on-street parking enforcement could move from Toronto Police to the Toronto Parking Authority. The framework sets policy directions and actions for managing parking as Toronto grows, tied to net-zero, land-use, and congestion goals.

title: Minimizing Salt Pollution that Poison Rivers and Streams
topics: pedestrian walkways, road safety, road salt management; footpaths; pedestrian ways; walking paths; walkways
brief: This member motion asks City Council to urge the Ontario minister to create limited liability protection for property owners who follow best practices for salt use, push for enforceable standards for salt contractors, and keep reducing the City's own road salt use. The motion says excess road salt damages Toronto's rivers and streams, is designated a toxic substance under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, and largely comes from heavy use by private contractors.

title: Toronto Parking Authority Security Approach and Framework
topics: parking, security, service delivery;
brief: The Toronto Parking Authority's report on its security approach and assessment framework for garages and parking lots — including findings from a community safety audit at Car Park 150 (40 Larch Street) — goes to City Council for information, along with keeping a related confidential attachment private as it concerns the security of City property. The report responds to Council's request for a universal security protocol. The Parking Authority has raised its annual security budget by $2.9 million since 2021 — a 290 per cent increase — to $3.9 million, allocated $4.1 million for CCTV across seven garages and $2.7 million for better vehicle and pedestrian access control, and plans another $25.7 million over the next five years.

title: Pedestrian Streets Policy and Guidelines Development - Accessibility Feedback
topics: accessibility, accessibility standards, city initiatives, pedestrians, policy development, transportation; accessibility legislation; aoda, barrier-free design; universal design; wheelchair accessible, city council priorities; corporate campaigns; council priorities; municipal initiatives, pedestrianization, policy making, transportation services
brief: Whether to request that City planning for car-free pedestrian streets include an analysis of alternative routes and accessible pick-up and drop-off areas within 30 metres of pedestrian zones, to support people with disabilities is before the committee. The recommendation comes from the Toronto Accessibility Advisory Committee, ahead of a new pedestrian streets policy being finalized in late 2025.

title: Automated Vehicle Pilot Deployment in Toronto Under the Highway Traffic Act
topics: motor vehicle safety regulations, motor vehicles, pilot projects; vehicles
brief: Whether to have staff report back by late 2026 on findings from Magna's provincially approved pilot testing driverless last-mile delivery vehicles on Toronto streets, and on what the City can learn about automated vehicles is before City Council. The pilot, approved under Ontario Regulation 306/15, uses three-wheeled vehicles up to 32 km/h on roads posted 40 km/h or less across all of Ward 9 and parts of Wards 4, 5, 11, and 12, with constant human oversight from a chase vehicle and a remote operator. The City has no regulatory authority over the pilot but submitted comments on safety.

title: Downtown Homelessness Addiction Recovery and Treatment (HART) Hub
topics: [activities in health], health, rehabilitation (people), substance abuse, supportive housing; alcohol abuse; drug abuse; drug addiction, alternative housing; special needs housing; supported housing, health coverage
brief: Creating the Downtown Homelessness and Addiction Recovery Treatment (HART) Hub — and authorizing the Medical Officer of Health to sign the agreements needed to set it up with health care and community partners — goes to City Council for approval. The City's application for the hub was approved in principle by the Ministry of Health on January 2, 2025. The hub aims to improve access to treatment and recovery services for people who use drugs, with connections to mental health care and housing supports.

title: Contract Amendment to Settle Legal Dispute with Innotex Inc., Concerning the Provision of Firefighter's Structural Bunker Suits
topics: contracts, fire and rescue services, firefighters, legal matters, personal protective equipment; fire fighters, fire fighting; fire services; fire suppression; firefighting; rescue; rescue operations; search and rescue, legal issues, ppe; protective clothing; protective devices; protective equipment
brief: Settling a legal dispute with Innotex Inc goes to City Council for approval. over the city's contract for firefighters' structural bunker suits. The City Solicitor, Fire Chief and Chief Procurement Officer recommend adopting confidential recommendations, with public release of those recommendations if adopted and the rest kept confidential as litigation-related. City Council decides.

title: Below Market Sublease / Lease Agreements with Various Child Care Services’ Operators - 15 York Garden Way, 135 Kyle Lowry Road, and 8450 Sheppard Avenue East
topics: child care facilities, city-owned properties, leasing, properties (real estate); child care agencies; child care centres; day cares; day nurseries; home care agencies; home child care providers; nursery schools, city owned properties; city properties, leases, property; real estate
brief: Approval of ten-year nominal sublease and lease agreements with three child care operators for newly built centres: the Canadian Mothercraft Society at 15 York Garden Way, the Child Development Institute at 135 Kyle Lowry Road, and Red Apple Day Care at 8450 Sheppard Avenue East inside the North East Scarborough Community Recreation Centre is before City Council. The operators were chosen through Children's Services expression-of-interest processes to run not-for-profit child care. City Council decides.

title: A Vision and Strategy for a Universal School Food Program in Toronto
topics: food, schools; community use of schools; educational institutions; school cafeterias; school classrooms; school gymnasiums, menus
brief: A universal school food program is taking shape. City Council is asked to request that Ontario increase and inflation-adjust its student nutrition funding to match the city's investment, to ask Ottawa for more National School Food Program funding, and to create a $7.492 million capital project for a universal morning meal program. The plan targets a universal morning meal in all Toronto school communities by the 2026/2027 school year and a universal lunch program no later than 2030. The project has cash flow commitments of $3.8 million in 2025 and $3.692 million in 2026. The city’s 2025 approved operating budget puts $31.1 million into the Student Nutrition Program — the investment council wants the province to match.

title: Assessment of City Impacts from Bill 17, Protect Ontario by Building Faster and Smarter Act, 2025 and Provincial Budget
topics: buildings, housing; homes; residences
brief: Bill 17's passage prompts a council response. City Council is asked to request that Ontario meaningfully consult city staff and the public before drafting regulations for Bill 17, the Protect Ontario by Building Faster and Smarter Act, 2025, to ask for a regulation permitting zoning with conditions, and to amend the development charges bylaw to remove mandatory indexing in 2025 and 2026. The province introduced Bill 17 on May 12, 2025, and moved it directly to third reading without further debate, committee review or public hearings; it received Royal Assent on June 5, 2025, before the public comment period closed on June 11. The report estimates the provincial changes could cost the city about $1.9 billion in cash flow over 10 years, mainly by deferring residential development charge payments until occupancy. Council adopted the item with an added request that Ontario make the city whole for those financial impacts and reconfigure the Building Faster Fund to provide funding upfront.

title: Commencing Public Consultations for Communities Impacted by New Shelter Locations - by Councillor James Pasternak, seconded by Councillor Parthi Kandavel

The sites are being developed under the city's 10-year Homelessness Services Capital Infrastructure Strategy. Council adopted the motion with an amendment that consultations happen if requested by the local councillor, and added a direction for staff to undertake a 'reset' of the community engagement process for the proposed shelter at 1220 Wilson Avenue, including liaising with the local councillor and addressing multilingual requirements before advancing construction at the site.

brief: Approval of in-year adjustments to the 2025 capital budget, offsetting $100.0 million in faster-spending projects with slower-spending ones, with no new debt is before the TTC Board. title: Revised Station Naming Policy
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, assets, subway stations; ttc
brief: Approval of a revised station naming policy that adds equity, diversity, inclusion and anti-racism considerations, sets clear naming criteria and formalizes how stations are named is before the TTC Board. Stations could be named or sponsored by major public sector institutions if they provide value reflecting the renaming costs, and the policy aligns with Metrolinx's naming principles for regional wayfinding. Staff do not recommend paid corporate naming rights, saying they could harm customer wayfinding and the public nature of the system.

title: Non-Fare Revenue Strategic Review
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, business incentives, economic development, public transit, revenue generation; business development; business opportunities; business retention; investment attraction; investment marketing, commercial facade improvement program; commercial festivals and special events program; commercial research program; community grant allocations; employment area revitalization; employment revitalization areas; facade improvement; financial incentives; mural program; streetscape improvement program, local transit; mass transit; public transport; public transportation; surface transit; transit; transit services; urban transportation, revenue tools, ttc
brief: Principles and a work plan for growing non-fare revenue, such as expanding advertising, partnerships, sponsorships and retail, would get the TTC Board's endorsement, along with setting up a dedicated team to carry out the plan. Staff do not recommend pursuing paid corporate station naming rights, citing low revenue potential, staffing demands, legal risks and impacts on customer experience. Non-fare revenue was about 7 percent of total TTC revenue in 2024, in line with peer agencies. The board also directed staff to explore opening a physical TTC store at Davisville Station or another central location, reporting back with costs, benefits and an implementation plan by the end of 2025.

title: Platform Edge Doors Study - Outcome of Feasibility and Business Case Studies
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, infrastructure, safety, subway stations; public safety, ttc
brief: A study on platform edge doors for subway stations is before the TTC Board, which would add platform door requirements to the TTC's design standards for future stations and seek budget funding for a pilot at TMU (Dundas) Station. The study assessed retrofitting 74 existing subway station platform levels across Lines 1, 2 and 4, concluding a one-size-fits-all approach will not work and each station's needs will drive the choice of technology. Platform doors are seen as a way to reduce track intrusions that disrupt service.
