brief: This is an administrative inquiry: Councillor James Pasternak (Ward 6, York Centre) is asking City staff for information on when by-laws to protect places of worship — sometimes called 'bubble zone' by-laws — will be brought back to Council. In December 2024, Council directed staff to prepare those by-laws by the end of March 2025, and councillors have been told that deadline will be missed.

title: Public Reporting of Performance and Service Standards
topics: annual reports, customer service, standards; annual financial reports; annual report cards; report cards
brief: Councillor Paul Ainslie is asking City Council to direct the Executive Director, Customer Experience, to report to the September 19, 2025 meeting of the General Government Committee on progress toward publicly reporting city divisions' performance against service standards by December 2025. Currently the Customer Experience Division does not post its performance against service targets on the city's website, though a tool is in development with no timeline. City Council decides.

title: 32 to 50 Larwood Boulevard - Expropriation of Portions of Properties - Stage 2
topics: expropriations, land acquisition, properties (real estate); compulsory purchase; eminent domain, land acquisitions; park acquisition; parkland acquisition; parks acquisitions; property acquisition; property acquisitions, property; real estate
brief: Up for approval at City Council: the second stage of expropriating parts of nine properties at 32 to 50 Larwood Boulevard for a multi-use trail improving pedestrian and cyclist safety on the east side of Brimley Road South, from Barkdene Hills to Bluffers Park Road. The trail is part of the city's multi-use trail network and the Scarborough Waterfront Project. City Council decides.

title: 75 Hyde Avenue - Expropriation of a Permanent Easement for the Construction of the Black Creek Sanitary Trunk Sewer Relief System - Stage 2
topics: expropriations, land acquisition, properties (real estate); compulsory purchase; eminent domain, land acquisitions; park acquisition; parkland acquisition; parks acquisitions; property acquisition; property acquisitions, property; real estate
brief: Whether to approve the second stage of expropriating a permanent easement on part of 75 Hyde Avenue for Toronto Water's Black Creek Sanitary Trunk Sewer Relief System is before City Council. The property owner initially requested an inquiry into whether the taking is fair, sound and reasonably necessary, but has since withdrawn that request, clearing the way for Council to approve. City Council decides.

title: 486 Front Street West - Below Market Sublease Agreement with Macaulay Centres for Children For Child Care Services
topics: child care facilities, leasing, operating budgets; child care agencies; child care centres; day cares; day nurseries; home care agencies; home child care providers; nursery schools, leases
brief: Approval of a ten-year nominal (below-market) sublease with Macaulay Centres for Children to run a new child care centre on the upper ground floor at 486 Front Street West, with occupancy expected in the third quarter of 2025 is before City Council. The operator was chosen through an expression-of-interest process run by Children's Services, and the city itself will hold a head lease with the developer for the space. The item affects child care availability in the downtown west area. City Council decides.

title: Potential Litigation Arising from the Construction of Certain Sanitary Sewer Upgrades in the Vicinity of 1215 York Mills Road
topics: construction, damages, sanitary sewers, sewers; building, sewage systems; sewerage
brief: Dealing with potential litigation over costs from sanitary sewer upgrades built by Alit Don Valley Property Inc goes to City Council for approval. near its development at 1215 York Mills Road. The City Solicitor's legal advice and recommended instructions sit in a confidential attachment, and Council is asked to adopt those confidential recommendations. City Council decides.

title: Suspension of Duron Ontario Ltd.
topics: contract termination, contracts, suspension, vendors;
brief: Suspending Duron Ontario Ltd goes to City Council for approval. from bidding on or being awarded any city contracts for five years, for contraventions of the Supplier Code of Conduct covering over-billing, double billing, keeping known over-payments, misleading or false claims, billing for goods not supplied, and professional misconduct. The recommendation comes from Corporate Real Estate Management and the Chief Procurement Officer. City Council decides.

title: Non-Competitive Contract with Comprint Systems Incorporated for Election Services Applications and Maintenance
topics: application software, contracts, software, system software; computer programs
brief: City Council faces a decision on approving a non-competitive six-year contract with Comprint Systems Incorporated for the election technology applications the City Clerk uses to update the voters list, manage 1,000-plus voting locations, run the MyVote elector portal, administer mail-in voting and track election-day issues. The contract would start no earlier than May 1, 2025, with options for four additional one-year renewals, supporting the 2026 and 2030 municipal and school board elections. The source documents list $9,485,507 ($9,652,452 net of HST recoveries) and $500,000. City Council decides.

title: Award of Provincial Vendor of Record and Non-competitive Procurement for the Supply of Paging and Mobile Devices, Accessories and Services
topics: agreements, purchasing, vendors; acquisition; buying; procurement; sourcing; tenders, tenancy agreements
brief: The city wants to adopt the Province of Ontario's Vendor of Record arrangement for mobile devices and services, with a total potential value of $69,476,714 ($70,669,504 net of HST recoveries) over up to nine years and three months, covering wireless service for more than 22,600 city staff. The city says it has saved over $10 million through the vendor-of-record approach since 2020 and expects another $16.5 million in savings and cost avoidance from 2025 to 2034. A separate non-competitive contract with Paging Network of Canada for pagers and paging services is also proposed at $1,500,000 ($1,526,400). The source documents also list $500,000, $57,484,224, $64,957,173, $58,495,946, $4,801,719, $5,425,942, $4,886,229, $1,800,361, $2,034,408, $1,832,048, $5,390,410, $6,091,163, $5,485,281 and $1,695,000. The item is before the General Government Committee, with City Council authority sought for the paging contract.

title: Award of Doc4747531748 to Walker Environmental Group Inc., for Processing Services for Yard Waste Material and Digester Solids Material for Solid Waste Management Services
topics: contracts, solid waste, solid waste management, waste, waste collection, yard waste, yard waste collection; collection (activity); collection routes, collection (activity); leaf vacuuming; mechanical leaf collection; mechanical leaf pickup; yard waste pickup, commercial waste; municipal solid waste; refuse, garden waste; yard rubbish, solid waste management planning; swm; waste management
brief: On the agenda at City Council: awarding a $24,311,595 contract ($24,739,479 net of HST recoveries) to Walker Environmental Group Inc., the lowest supplier meeting specifications, to process up to 40,000 tonnes of yard waste and 25,000 tonnes of digester solids a year, with haulage by the City. The contract runs three years with options for two additional one-year extensions. City Council decides on the award.

title: Non-Competitive Contract with Teleflex Medical Canada Inc., for the Supply and Delivery of Medical Supplies and Equipment for Toronto Paramedic Services
topics: operating budgets, paramedics, purchasing; acquisition; buying; procurement; sourcing; tenders
brief: Toronto Paramedic Services wants a $340,713 non-competitive contract ($346,710 net of HST recoveries) with Teleflex Medical Canada, its existing supplier of specialized medical supplies and equipment for tactical paramedics, CBRNE and heavy urban search and rescue teams. The contract would run June 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, with four optional one-year extensions, and the source documents also list $500,000. City Council decides.

title: 2972 Islington Avenue - Application for a Clothing Drop Box Location Permit
topics: applications, clothing drop boxes; application process, clothes donation boxes; clothing bins
brief: Council decides on another clothing drop box. Council is asked to decide whether to allow a clothing donation drop box at 2972 Islington Avenue: Municipal Licensing and Standards refused the permit, so council must choose to uphold the refusal or approve the permit application.

title: Assumption of Services for Lowe's Company Canada, 66M-2498, 08 195178 WET 02 SB, Lowe's Place
topics: assumption of services, municipal services; city services
brief: The city is taking over roads in a Lowe's subdivision. Council is asked to formally take over the roads and municipal services in the Lowe's subdivision at 50 Resources Road (Plan 66M-2498, dated June 2012), release the developer's performance guarantee, and pass an assumption by-law for the public highway and services.

title: 56, 58 and 60 Fieldway Road - Community Benefits Charge In-Kind Report
topics: community benefits, rezoning; re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: Public art could stand in for a cash development charge. Council is asked to let the developer at 56, 58, and 60 Fieldway Road provide on-site public art as part of its Community Benefits Charge, up to 33 percent of the charge, instead of cash, with the balance due when building permits are issued. The mixed-use development with four towers and a public park was approved in October 2023.

title: Lake Shore Boulevard West between Royal York Road and Lake Crescent - On-Street Accessible Loading Zone
topics: accessibility, loading zones; barrier-free design; universal design; wheelchair accessible, drop off areas; drop off zones; loading spaces; pick up areas; pick up zones
brief: An accessible loading zone is proposed on Lake Shore Boulevard West. Council is asked to approve an on-street accessible loading zone on the north side of Lake Shore Boulevard West east of Royal York Road, operating at all times, giving a resident unimpeded curbside access to TTC Wheel-Trans service. TTC transit service on the street requires council approval.

title: Evans Avenue - Heavy Trucks
topics: heavy trucks, motor vehicles; vehicles
brief: The overnight truck ban stays as is. Council is asked not to extend the heavy-truck ban on Evans Avenue between Islington Avenue and Royal York Road to all hours, as staff's review does not support an around-the-clock ban; the current 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. restriction would stay. TTC transit service on the street requires council approval.

title: 455 Sentinel Road - Application for a Clothing Drop Box Location Permit
topics: applications, clothing drop boxes; application process, clothes donation boxes; clothing bins
brief: Another clothing drop box permit is council's call. Council is asked to decide whether to allow a clothing donation drop box at 455 Sentinel Road: Municipal Licensing and Standards refused the permit, so council must choose to uphold the refusal or approve the permit application.

title: 345 Driftwood Avenue - Application for a Clothing Drop Box Location Permit
topics: clothing drop boxes; clothes donation boxes; clothing bins
brief: A clothing drop box permit is council's call. Council is asked to decide whether to allow a clothing donation drop box at 345 Driftwood Avenue: Municipal Licensing and Standards refused the permit, so council must choose to uphold the refusal or approve the permit application.

title: 464 Royal York Road - Official Plan Amendment and Zoning Amendment Application - Appeal Report
topics: Official Plans, zoning bylaws; zoning by-laws; zoning bylaw project; zoning project
brief: Another rental building is headed to the Tribunal. Council is asked to direct the City Solicitor and staff to oppose a 12-storey rental building with 112 homes at 464 Royal York Road, in its current form, at the Ontario Land Tribunal, appealed after council missed its decision deadline, while talks continue. The proposal includes a publicly accessible area with a pedestrian walkway connection to Royal York Road.

title: Building a Universal Student Food Program in Toronto
topics: food, nutrition, students; diet; dieting; healthy eating, menus
brief: School food funding is the ask here. City Council is asked to request that the federal government reallocate unspent National Student Food Program funding for the 2025 budget year from jurisdictions without agreements in place to jurisdictions with agreements, including Toronto's school food programs, and to ask the Ontario government to increase its per-student contributions to student nutrition programs. The item comes from the City-School Boards Advisory Committee. Council already increased the 2025 operating budget by $5 million to expand the school food program.

title: Municipal Diversity Plan for Appointments to the Toronto Police Service Board and Police Board Composition
topics: appointments, police services boards; police boards
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to adopt a Municipal Diversity Plan for appointments to the Toronto Police Service Board, as required by section 28 of the Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019.

title: Rexdale - Casino Woodbine Community Benefits Agreement: 2024 Progress Update
topics: casinos, community benefits;
brief: The Casino Woodbine community benefits deal gets its 2024 check-in. City Council is asked to direct staff to negotiate updated definitions of the Woodbine Local Area and Equity Deserving Communities with One Toronto Gaming, and to authorize the City Manager to sign an amending agreement under the Rexdale-Casino Woodbine Community Benefits Agreement. The agreement, adopted in 2018, channels gaming expansion at Woodbine Racetrack into equity-focused community benefits, and the report cites figures of $100.5 million and $1.8 million in connection with the city's gaming revenue share.

title: Extending Vehicle Age Limits for Vehicles-for-Hire
topics: accessible taxicabs, taxicabs; cabs; taxi fares; taxis
brief: Taxis and limos could stay on the road longer. City Council is asked to amend the vehicles-for-hire bylaw so wheelchair accessible taxis and private transportation vehicles can be up to ten model years old, and to let sedan taxis and limousines due for replacement by March 31, 2025 keep operating until August 29, 2025. The motion follows industry concerns that 45 wheelchair accessible vehicles, about 10 percent of the fleet, are due to expire this year with 203 more next year, while also extending the rules for all sedan taxis and limos in the same position.

title: Transit Priority on Queens Quay East - Interim Priority Bus Lanes
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, light rail transit, transportation; lrt, transportation services, ttc
brief: Temporary bus lanes are proposed ahead of the waterfront light rail. City Council is asked to authorize interim priority bus lanes on Queens Quay East, Parliament Street, and Front Street West, to improve transit travel times and reliability for about 4,000 daily customers ahead of the Waterfront East LRT. The TTC Board endorsed the measures in February 2025. The measures would cost an estimated $800,000 in capital funding, covered under the TTC's 2025–2034 capital budget.

title: Toronto Ferry Service Operational Review
topics: ferries, safety, water transportation; ferry boats; ferryboats, marine transportation; maritime transport; water transport, public safety
brief: The Island ferry system's future operations are under review. City Council is asked to direct the Deputy City Manager, Corporate Services, to report back to the Executive Committee by the fourth quarter of 2025 on progress implementing the Toronto Ferry Service operational review, which is examining the organizational structure for the ferry system, the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal, and the Island ferry docks. It matters to the Torontonians and visitors who rely on the ferries.

title: Mayor’s Economic Action Plan in Response to United States Tariffs
topics: [activities in planning and development], economic development, taxes; business development; business opportunities; business retention; investment attraction; investment marketing, levies
brief: The city's response to US tariffs is up for adoption. City Council is asked to adopt the Mayor's Economic Action Plan in Response to US Tariffs, to direct the City Manager to keep the plan current, and to report to the July Executive Committee with an implementation update and any new long-term actions. The plan responds to tariffs and trade threats from the new US administration that have shaken Canada's economic relationship with the US. The financial impact section puts staffing and expertise costs for the plan's immediate actions at $2.4 million, to be covered within existing budgets.

title: Participation in Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Cities Initiative Advocacy Days and Advocacy Against Tariffs
topics: economy, environment (sc);
brief: This is a procedural item: Councillor Ainslie reports on representing the city at the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence Cities Initiative Advocacy Days in Washington, D.C., March 5 to 7, 2025, where Canadian and American mayors advocated for the watershed and against tariffs threatening cross-border trade. Council is asked to receive the report for information.

title: Amending the Housing Rights Advisory Committee Terms of Reference
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to amend the Housing Rights Advisory Committee's terms of reference so it can form informal working groups of up to five members, with staff support from the Housing Secretariat. The committee advises council on advancing the right to adequate housing in Toronto.

title: FIFA World Cup 2026 Toronto: Economic Benefits of Hosting, Soccer for All Legacy Fund and Community Benefits Plan Updates
topics: financial reports, sports, sports tournaments; annual financial reports; financial statements, tournaments
brief: More World Cup spending is on the table. City Council is asked to increase the 2025 operating budget by $10.7 million from the Major Special Event Reserve Fund to advance World Cup hospitality, and to authorize staff to accept donations for the Soccer for All Legacy Fund, including up to 12 mini-pitches. The item also shares data on the economic, social, and cultural opportunities of hosting the tournament and sets up quarterly reporting on community benefits. Council would also reaffirm its commitment to deliver the tournament within its $380 million budget.

title: Supporting Ownership Housing Developments
topics: development, housing, ownership housing; developing land; development (land); land development, homes; residences
brief: Stalled condo projects could get a push. City Council is asked to direct staff to review stalled condo development applications that include 5 to 10 percent affordable housing and to approve supports for up to 3,000 ownership units, prioritizing projects with more affordable housing. The item responds to a housing supply slowdown driven by high construction and financing costs, higher interest rates, and declining pre-construction sales. The financial impact section estimates up to $182.1 million in deferred development-charge payments, plus $28.3 million in foregone investment returns.

title: Advancing the Tamil Community Centre
brief: A non-profit Tamil Community Centre in northeast Scarborough is getting a fee break. City Council is asked to waive city planning application fees for the Official Plan and Zoning By-law amendments needed for the centre at 311 Staines Road, an area lacking city-owned community centres, advanced by the Canadian Tamil community's steering committee after more than a decade of foundational work. The report cites a $26.3 million figure and a $1 figure in connection with the project.

title: Public Reporting of Performance and Service Standards
topics: customers, standards;
brief: City service performance could become more public. City Council is asked to direct all city divisions to share performance data with the Customer Experience Division so it can publicly report on service standards, maintain user-friendly public dashboards, and report on trends twice a year. The item follows a Service Excellence Committee recommendation from Councillor Paul Ainslie.

title: Increasing Number of Meetings Per Year for the Confronting Anti-Black Racism Advisory Committee
topics: committee meetings, meetings;
brief: An advisory committee could meet more often. The Executive Committee is asked to recommend that council amend the terms of reference of the Confronting Anti-Black Racism Advisory Committee so it holds up to six meetings per year instead of up to four. The recommendation comes from the committee itself via Councillor Amber Morley.

title: Review of Toronto’s Winter Maintenance Program
topics: maintenance, snow removal, winter; snow melting; windrow clearing (snow)
brief: The February 2025 snowstorms triggered a call for a full review of winter maintenance. City Council is asked to request a review of winter maintenance operations after the storms, to investigate the gap between reported and actual sidewalk clearing, and to check whether private snow removal contractors met their contract obligations. The motion cites residents, including seniors, people with mobility issues, and parents with strollers, left contending with a slow city response.

title: Developing an Urgent Downtown Coyote Action Plan
topics: wildlife; bats; coyotes; deer; foxes; raccoons; skunks; snakes; wild animals
brief: Downtown coyote encounters have prompted a call for an urgent action plan. The item asks council to direct staff to distribute public education material to downtown residents on coyote safety, and to urgently develop a Downtown Coyote Action Plan, ahead of the city's updated coyote strategy planned for the fourth quarter of 2025. The motion points to attacks on dogs and fear among residents in densely populated downtown communities with limited green space.

title: Waiving Permit Fee Charges for the 2025 Bum Run in Support of Colon Cancer Awareness
topics: [events in community and life], community outreach, fees, permits; administrative fees; admission fees; admission prices; rates; service charges; user charges; user fees, awareness programs; community engagement; outreach; promotion (communication); public outreach, permit renewal
brief: A charity run for colon cancer awareness is getting its city permit fees waived. Council is asked to waive permit fee charges of $5,304.49 and $303.15 for the 2025 Bum Run, a volunteer-run, non-profit event raising awareness and funds for colon cancer early diagnosis, which would normally pay to close or occupy city roads. The event has run for thirteen years, noting that 90 percent of colon cancer deaths are preventable through early diagnosis.

title: Toronto Community Housing Tenant Engagement System and Implementation Plan
topics: housing, tenants; homes; residences, renters; tenancy agreements
brief: This is an information item: the Toronto Community Housing board approved a new Engage Together tenant engagement model and a phased workplan to replace the current model, and forwarded the report to council for information. No decision is proposed at council.

title: Proposed Pilot for Non-Motorized Mobile Food Vendors in University-Rosedale
topics: food, vendor permits, vendors; menus
brief: Food carts could get a pilot program in University-Rosedale. Council is asked to amend the street vending bylaw to allow a pilot permitting non-motorized food vendors to operate in mobile vending zones in Ward 11. The city's street vending rules, Chapter 740, are under review through 2025.

title: York-Eglinton Business Improvement Area - Name Change
topics: business improvement areas, economic development; bia; business improvement associations, business development; business opportunities; business retention; investment attraction; investment marketing
brief: A BIA name change reflecting the neighbourhood's identity is before council. Council is asked to approve renaming the York-Eglinton Business Improvement Area to the Little Jamaica Business Improvement Area. The BIA's board of management voted to support the renaming and its membership endorsed it at the 2024 annual general meeting.

title: Proposed Upper Avenue Business Improvement Area Poll Results
topics: business improvement areas, polling; bia; business improvement associations
brief: Businesses along Avenue Road could get their own Business Improvement Area. Council is asked to designate the area along Avenue Road from Lawrence Avenue West to Joicey Boulevard as the Upper Avenue Business Improvement Area, after the City Clerk conducted a poll showing the required support from local businesses. A BIA lets local businesses fund shared streetscape and marketing improvements through a levy.

title: Authority to Enter into a Multi-Year Agreement with Toronto Arts Council (2025-2029)
topics: agreements, arts and culture; tenancy agreements
brief: The city's arts funding relationship is up for renewal. Council is asked to authorize a new five-year agreement with the Toronto Arts Council for 2025-2029, under which the independent organization distributes cultural grants to non-profit organizations and individuals on the city's behalf. The current agreement expires March 31, 2025, and the new one includes updated reporting and a framework for shared funding priorities.

title: Parkland obligations at 25 Fisherville Road - by Councillor James Pasternak, seconded by Councillor Mike Colle
topics: land acquisition, parkland dedication, parks; conservation areas; greenbelts; parkland, land acquisitions; park acquisition; parkland acquisition; parks acquisitions; property acquisition; property acquisitions
brief: Whether to give a developer more time to hand over parkland at 25 Fisherville Road goes to council. The member motion asks council to allow the required parkland dedication of 397 square metres, plus a 133 square metre over-dedication, for the redevelopment to be transferred to the city within 36 months of the first above-grade building permit, rather than at the usual earlier timing. The redevelopment was approved through an Ontario Land Tribunal settlement in 2021, with a final order in 2022 resulting in zoning amendment 335-2024. Council adopted the item with an amendment permitting the future park and street lands to be used for stockpiling soils or materials and as an interim construction staging area, subject to agreements with the city on insurance, tree removal and replacement, duration, and restoration.

title: 40-60 St. Lawrence Avenue - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions
topics: planning tribunals; omb; ontario municipal board
brief: This is a legal directions item: the City Solicitor is asking council for confidential instructions on the Ontario Land Tribunal hearing for the residential development proposal at 40-60 St. Lawrence Avenue. The applications, dating to October 2014, sought to amend Site and Area Specific Policy 6 of the Official Plan and the former Etobicoke zoning by-law for lands including the former 1061 The Queensway site. The legal advice stays confidential.

title: 266 and 268 Royal York Road - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions
topics: official plan amendments, planning tribunals; omb; ontario municipal board
brief: This is a legal directions item: council's instructions to the City Solicitor stay confidential. The Ontario Land Tribunal case concerns 266 and 268 Royal York Road, where the applicant proposed a mixed-use development with 37-storey and 23-storey residential towers plus ground-floor retail and a self-storage warehouse, then appealed after the city did not decide. The ruling will determine what gets built on the site.

title: 6212-6600 Yonge Street - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions
topics: official plan amendments, planning tribunals; omb; ontario municipal board
brief: This is a legal directions item: council's instructions to the City Solicitor stay confidential. The Ontario Land Tribunal case concerns the Centerpoint Mall redevelopment at 6212-6600 Yonge Street, where the applicant proposed buildings from 4 to 50 storeys with 635,766 square metres of residential floor area and a public park, under a site-specific policy. The outcome shapes one of North York's largest redevelopment sites.

title: Appointment of a Public Member to the Dangerous Dog Review Tribunal
topics: advisory committees, dogs; ad hoc committees; advisory groups; council reference groups; liaison committees; panels; political reference groups; public advisory committees; reference groups; round tables; roundtables; special committees; steering committees; sub-committees; subcommittees; task forces; working groups
brief: This is an appointments item: one seat on the Dangerous Dog Review Tribunal. Following a recommendation from the nominating panel, council is asked to appoint Sophia Davis to the tribunal for a term running March 28, 2025 to November 14, 2026. The tribunal hears appeals of dangerous dog designations, and further candidate details are confidential.

title: Review of Councillor Remuneration
topics: councillors, payment; aldermen; alderwomen; city councellors; city councillors; council members; councilors; members of council, paying; payment information; payment methods; payment options; pre-authorized payment plans; pre-authorized plans; preauthorized payments
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to receive it for information. The report advises that the City Manager and Chief People Officer will submit a report on a review of councillor remuneration before the March 26-28, 2025 council meeting, when any changes to councillor pay would be considered. No decision is proposed at this stage.

title: Recruitment for the Deputy City Manager, Community and Social Services
topics: cluster divisions, hiring process; hiring; job recall; recruitment; selection
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to receive it for information. The report advises that the City Manager will submit an update on the recruitment for the Deputy City Manager, Community and Social Services position before the March 26-28, 2025 council meeting. No decision is proposed.

title: Update on Electric Ferries Shoreside Infrastructure and Ferry Terminal Improvement Projects
topics: electricity, terminals, transportation infrastructure, transportation infrastructure management; electric power; electricity usage, intermodal stations; intermodal terminals; terminal stations; terminus; terminuses, road management; transportation operations, transportation network; transportation networks
brief: This is a procedural item: no decision is proposed. The report simply advises that the City Manager will submit an update on the electric ferries shoreside infrastructure and the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal improvement projects to the March 26-28, 2025 council meeting. The shoreside infrastructure project has a base budget of $42,535,680 (net of HST recoveries) for its three-year project management, design, build and commissioning agreement, with further financial details to come in a supplementary report. Council is asked to receive the notice for information.

title: Results of Collective Bargaining Negotiations Between the City of Toronto and CUPE Local 79
topics: agreements, labour relations, unions; collective bargaining; employee relations; labor relations; union-management relations, labour unions; trade unions, tenancy agreements
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to receive the report for information, with no decision proposed. The four collective agreements between CUPE Local 79, the union for the city's inside workers, and the City of Toronto expired December 31, 2024, and bargaining that began that month produced four tentative agreements on March 8, 2025, pending ratification. The outcome sets wages and working conditions for thousands of city staff.

title: Identifying and Addressing Pressures in the Refugee and Emergency Shelter System
topics: housing; homes; residences
brief: The latest picture of Toronto's shelter system, which is under sustained pressure, goes to council for consideration. Refugee claimants and asylum seekers in city shelters have risen from an average of 2,329 a night in March 2020 to 4,181 a night in March this year, while the city consistently shelters 4,900 to 6,400 people experiencing homelessness each night. The item asks council to consider reports and communications on fair access to the shelter and housing system.

title: 604 Bay Street - Notice of Intention to Designate a Property under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act
topics: heritage designation;
brief: Downtown's 604 Bay Street is a step closer to heritage protection. Council is asked to state its intention to designate the property at 604 Bay Street, including the 610 Bay Street entrance, under Part IV, Section 29 of the Ontario Heritage Act for its cultural heritage value. If no objections are filed, a designation bylaw will follow, which would protect the building's heritage attributes.

title: 2636-2654 Eglinton Avenue West and 1856 and 1856A Keele Street - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions
topics: appeals, planning tribunals, rezoning; omb; ontario municipal board, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: This is a legal directions item: the City Solicitor needs private directions. The Ontario Land Tribunal case concerns 2636-2654 Eglinton Avenue West and 1856 and 1856A Keele Street, where the applicant proposed a 33-storey mixed-use building and appealed after council did not decide. The ruling will shape what gets built at Eglinton and Keele.

title: 137-141 Isabella Street - Ontario Land Tribunal Hearing - Request for Directions
topics: planning tribunals, rezoning; omb; ontario municipal board, re-zoning; zoning by-law amendment applications; zoning bylaw amendments
brief: This is a legal directions item: council's instructions stay confidential. The Ontario Land Tribunal case concerns 137-141 Isabella Street, where the applicant proposed a 69-storey residential tower with 823 homes, including 61 replacement rental units, then appealed after council did not decide. The outcome affects housing supply and rental replacement in the area.

title: Authority to Negotiate Agreements Related to Queen’s Park North Through Philanthropic Partnerships in Alignment with City of Toronto Priorities
topics: [activities in law], agreements; tenancy agreements
brief: A $50 million private donation could reshape Queen's Park North. Council is asked to authorize the General Manager of Parks and Recreation to negotiate and sign a donation agreement with the Weston Foundations for community engagement on improvements to Queen's Park North, the historic park dedicated in 1860 and leased to the city by the University of Toronto. The move, recommended by the Mayor, would pair philanthropic money with city priorities for one of Toronto's most prominent green spaces.

title: Appointment of a Public Member to the Toronto Transit Commission board
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, public appointments; ttc
brief: One step in filling a public seat on the TTC board. The Civic Appointments Committee will interview candidates and recommend one public member for City Council to appoint to the Toronto Transit Commission board, for a term ending March 29, 2029. Candidate details are kept confidential.

title: Introduction of General Bills and Confirming Bills
topics: by-laws; bylaws
brief: This is a procedural item: City Council will introduce general bills and confirming bills, the formal step that turns approved decisions into official city bylaws. No new policy is decided here.

title: Award of Doc4467832078 to iManage LLC for the Provision of Electronic Legal Document Management System (LDMS) for Legal Services Division
topics: purchasing, records; acquisition; buying; procurement; sourcing; tenders
brief: A five-year contract to iManage LLC for a legal document management system that stores emails and documents in a single searchable file per case for Legal Services, from April 1, 2025 to January 20, 2030, is up for approval by the Bid Award Panel. The contract award value is $1,504,816 net of all applicable taxes and charges, including 20 per cent for miscellaneous items ($1,700,442 including HST and all applicable charges; $1,531,301 net of HST recoveries).

brief: A three-year contract to Kudlak-Baird (1982) Limited for maintenance and repair of electrical systems at various city buildings, from April 1, 2025 to March 31, 2028, with one optional renewal year, is up for approval by the Bid Award Panel. The award value is $9,681,642 net of all applicable taxes and charges ($10,940,255 including HST and all applicable charges; $9,852,039 net of HST recoveries); the option-year value is $3,324,030 ($3,756,154; $3,382,533); and the four-year total is $13,005,672 ($14,696,410,; $13,234,572). brief: A contract to D. Crupi & Sons Limited for interim repairs, permanent restorations and maintenance of arterial, collector and local roads and laneways in the Etobicoke York district (Wards 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 9), running through December 31, 2025, is up for approval by the Bid Award Panel. The contract award value is $1,817,777 net of all applicable taxes and charges ($2,054,088 including HST and all applicable charges; $1,849,770 net of HST recoveries). Bids received: $1,787,777.07, $1,927,145.06, $1,998,412.00, $2,110,718.85, $2,187,639.82 and $2,371,523.41.

brief: A contract to PNJ Engineering Inc. for material specification compliance testing and project quality assurance services on road projects in the Toronto-East York and Scarborough districts, through December 31, 2025, with one optional renewal year, is up for approval by the Bid Award Panel. The award value is $326,565 net of all applicable taxes and charges ($369,018 including HST and all applicable charges; $332,313 net of HST recoveries); the option-year value is $336,062 ($379,750; $341,977); and the two-year total is $662,627 ($748,768; $674,289). brief: A contract to 614128 Ontario Ltd. o/a Trisan Construction to replace the sanitary sewer line serving the Bluffer's Park washroom, expected to finish by August 31, 2025, is up for approval by the Bid Award Panel. The contract award value is $1,661,803 net of all applicable taxes and charges ($1,877,837 including HST and all applicable charges; $1,691,051 net of HST recoveries). Bids received: $1,326,992.90, $1,694,478.00, $2,974,974.00, $3,329,260.00 and $3,605,426.25.

title: Award of Doc4837489444 to WSP Canada Inc. for the Preliminary, Detailed Design, Construction and Post Construction Services for the Queensway Project for Engineering and Construction Services
topics: construction, engineering, purchasing; acquisition; buying; procurement; sourcing; tenders, building
brief: A contract to WSP Canada Inc. for engineering services for the preliminary, detailed design, construction and post-construction phases of the Queensway project, running through December 31, 2031, is up for approval by the Bid Award Panel. The contract award value is $5,307,875 net of all applicable taxes and charges ($5,997,899 including HST and all applicable charges; $5,401,294 net of HST recoveries).

title: Arenas - 2023 Audited Financial Statements and Status of Outstanding 2023 Audited Financial Statements
topics: arenas, audits, financial reports; annual financial reports; financial statements, auditors; auditors, indoor hockey rinks; rinks
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to receive the 2023 audited financial statements and management letters for the North Toronto Memorial Arena and the William H. Bolton Arena, for information. Three other 2023 arena statements were presented earlier in 2024, and three are still in progress. No policy change is proposed.

title: City of Toronto’s Modular Housing Initiative: The Need to Balance Fast Delivery with Stronger Management of Contracts and Costs - Management Status Update on Recommendations
topics: audits, buildings, construction, contracts, costs, dwellings, housing; auditors; auditors, building, homes; residences
brief: This is a procedural item: council is asked to receive a status update on how the Housing Secretariat and Corporate Real Estate Management are carrying out the Auditor General's 20 recommendations for managing modular housing project contracts and costs. No new decision is proposed.

title: Securing Online Confidential Committee and Board Meetings: Sharing Best Practices at the City, and its Agencies and Corporations
topics: committee meetings, confidentiality, council meetings, meetings, public meetings;
brief: The Auditor General reviewed cybersecurity for confidential online committee and board meetings and recommends stronger, standardized guidance and training on starting and running them securely, to be shared with the city's agencies and corporations. Council is asked to have staff put the changes in place. This affects the confidentiality of closed-door meetings.

title: Audit of Parks Branch Operations - Phase 2: Supporting Vibrant Parks by Improving Park Asset Management and Repair Processes
topics: administration, assessment, assets, audits, maintenance, management (activity); auditors; auditors
brief: The Auditor General's phase 2 review of the parks branch, which maintains more than 1,500 city parks, recommends better monitoring of park inspections and deficiency follow-up, more consistent repair-related service requests and work-order tracking, and a comprehensive system for tracking public complaints. Council is asked to have staff implement the changes. This affects how quickly park problems get fixed across the city.

title: Audit of Toronto Shelter and Support Services - Warming Centres and Winter Respite Sites: Understanding and Addressing Demand While Improving Financial Accountability to Stretch Dollars Further
topics: audits, housing, warming centres, women; auditors; auditors, homes; residences, shelters for women
brief: The Auditor General audited the city's winter shelter programs — warming centres and winter respite sites — and recommends better ways to measure unmet demand and manage bed vacancies, so funding stretches further and more people experiencing homelessness can get indoors in winter. Council is asked to direct shelter services staff to carry out the recommendations. This affects winter survival services for people experiencing homelessness from November 15 to April 15.

title: Auditor General's 2024 Annual Report on the Fraud and Waste Hotline
topics: audits, crime reporting, fraud, information services, waste; access toronto; help lines; helplines; hotlines; inquiries; inquiry services; referral services; telephone hotlines, anonymous crime reporting; crime stoppers; crime tips, auditors; auditors, waste (fraud)
brief: The 2024 annual report on the Fraud and Waste Hotline goes to Council for information: 679 complaints (about 1,050 allegations) were received, down about 36 per cent from 2023. The program helped prevent $2.0 million in actual losses plus $1.1 million in potential losses between 2020 and 2024. No decision is proposed.

title: Auditor General's 2024 Annual Report - Demonstrating the Value of the Auditor General's Office
topics: annual reports, audits, information; annual financial reports; annual report cards; report cards, auditors; auditors
brief: The Auditor General's 2024 annual report goes to Council for information. It reports that the office's 2024 work — 10 audit, investigation and cybersecurity reports with 86 recommendations — has produced savings projected over five years totalling over $376 million, against a 2020–2024 office operating cost of about $33.3 million, or about $11 back for every dollar invested. No decision is proposed.

title: Fare Compliance Action Plan - Update
body: Toronto Transit Commission - Audit, Finance and Risk Management Committee
topics: compliance, enforcement, payment; paying; payment information; payment methods; payment options; pre-authorized payment plans; pre-authorized plans; preauthorized payments
brief: This is a procedural item: the TTC's Audit and Risk Management Committee will receive a confidential in-camera presentation updating the Fare Compliance Action Plan. The material stays private because it concerns the security of municipal property, and the committee is asked to authorize that confidentiality. No policy change is proposed in this item.

title: Audit, Risk, and Compliance - 2025 Audit Plan and Departmental Evaluation
body: Toronto Transit Commission - Audit, Finance and Risk Management Committee
topics: audits; auditors; auditors
brief: The TTC's Audit and Risk Management Committee will consider approving the 2025 internal audit plan and an updated audit charter for the TTC's Audit, Risk and Compliance department. The proposed plan consists of four full assurance projects and four follow-up validation projects, aimed at improving efficiency, compliance and decision-making. The results would be reported back to the committee.

title: Audit, Risk and Compliance - 2025 Enterprise Risk Management Update
body: Toronto Transit Commission - Audit, Finance and Risk Management Committee
brief: The TTC's Audit and Risk Management Committee will consider changes to the TTC's enterprise risk management framework and receive a status update on the program, including a confidential portion that stays private because it concerns the security of TTC property. The only change proposed is adding a vision statement to the framework, which the committee approved in March 2024, in line with consultant recommendations. The report also lays out the 2025 roadmap and a multi-year plan for developing the program.

title: Audit, Risk and Compliance - 2024 Audit Plan Status Update
body: Toronto Transit Commission - Audit, Finance and Risk Management Committee
topics: audits, compliance; auditors; auditors
brief: This is a procedural item: the TTC's Audit and Risk Management Committee is asked to receive a status update on the 2024 audit plan for information. The update reports three final reports issued and fieldwork essentially complete on two more projects. The committee would also authorize keeping a confidential attachment private because it concerns the security of municipal property.

title: Executive Compliance Certificates - CEO Submission (2024)
body: Toronto Transit Commission - Audit, Finance and Risk Management Committee
topics: compliance, legislation, provincial legislation, regulations; acts
brief: This is a procedural item: the TTC's Audit and Risk Management Committee is asked to receive the CEO's 2024 executive compliance certificates for information. The certificates, introduced in 2020, are how TTC executives formally confirm compliance with laws and regulations, flagging any non-compliance and areas that could use procedural improvement. No policy change is proposed.

title: Audit of the Toronto Transit Commission’s Non-Union Workforce Planning and Management
body: Toronto Transit Commission - Audit, Finance and Risk Management Committee
topics: audits, human resources, labour force; auditors; auditors, labor force; workforce
brief: The TTC's Audit and Risk Management Committee will consider the Auditor General's audit of how the TTC plans and manages its non-union workforce. In 2024 the TTC averaged 16,300 full-time employees, of whom 4,000 were non-union; about 15 percent of non-union staff will be eligible for retirement by the end of 2025, rising to 21 percent by the end of 2027, and over 600 non-union employees left voluntarily between 2019 and 2023. The audit calls for clearer workforce planning as the TTC faces growing difficulty attracting and keeping non-union staff amid strong labour competition.

title: Appeal of the Chief Building Official's Decision for a Sign Variance Application for One First Party Ground Sign at 40 Humewood Drive
topics: signs; signage
brief: A property owner is appealing the Chief Building Official's decision on a sign variance for a ground sign at 40 Humewood Drive, intended to identify the Abiona Centre, a registered charity. The official refused the proposed variance but approved a different, CBO-designed variance with conditions such as limiting illumination between 9:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. The Sign Variance Committee is being asked to decide the appeal.

title: Application for One Variance, Subject to Seven Conditions, Respecting One Third Party Electronic Ground Sign - 4711 Steeles Avenue East
topics: election signs, signs; signage
brief: PATTINSON Outdoor Advertising Limited Partnership is seeking an exception to the sign rules so the Chief Building Official can permit a double-faced third party electronic ground sign at 4711 Steeles Avenue East in Scarborough. City staff recommend the Sign Variance Committee approve the exception, subject to seven conditions.

title: Application for Two Variances, Each Subject to Four conditions, Respecting One Third Party Electronic Wall Sign - 11 Bay Street
topics: applications, sign permits, signs; application process, billboard permits; permanent sign permits; sign variances; street banner permits; temporary sign permits, signage
brief: Zelinka Priamo Ltd is seeking exceptions to the sign rules so the Chief Building Official can permit a third party electronic wall sign at 11 Bay Street. The sign would sit within 130 metres of the F.G. Gardiner Expressway, in an area where third-party signs are not permitted within 400 metres of the Expressway. City staff recommend the Sign Variance Committee refuse the exceptions.

title: Application for Two Variances, each Subject to Three Conditions, Respecting the Modification of One Third Party Electronic Roof Sign - 304 Yonge Street

title: Signage to Identify Privately Owned Publicly-Accessible Spaces
brief: Older privately owned public spaces, the plazas and forecourts secured before the 2014 POPS design guidelines, could get city signage pointing them out. The ask is a feasibility report, and it matters to anyone who would use these often-hard-to-spot public spaces.

title: FIFA World Cup 2026 Toronto: Economic Benefits of Hosting, Soccer for All Legacy Fund and Community Benefits Plan Updates
topics: community benefits, sports, sports tournaments; tournaments
brief: City Council is being asked to increase the 2025 operating budget by $10.7 million gross, fully funded by the Major Special Event Reserve Fund, to advance FIFA World Cup 2026 preparations. Staff are also reporting to the FIFA World Cup 2026 Subcommittee on the economic, social and cultural opportunities of hosting the tournament, with a focus on turning the event into long-term benefits for the Greater Toronto Area, the province and the country. The update also covers the Soccer for All Legacy Fund and the Community Benefits Plan, including a new framework for quarterly reporting on community benefits, local employment, equity-deserving communities and social procurement.

title: Investing In Youth, Empowering Our City’s Potential: Creation of a Toronto Youth Employment Program
topics: employment opportunities, youth, youth programs; adolescents, careers; employment; job applications; job boards; job openings; job opportunities; job postings; job vacancies; jobs; vacancies (jobs), leadership programs
brief: A proposal for a Toronto Youth Employment Program is before the Economic and Community Development Committee. The member motion asks the committee to recommend that council request an additional federal investment in the Canada Summer Jobs program for the City of Toronto to run the program, and a provincial investment for the same purpose, and to direct staff to create a multi-sector, career-focused youth employment strategy in 2025. The staff report notes the federal government proposed a $200.5 million investment for 2025-26 in the Canada Summer Jobs program nationally, but says dedicated funding is needed for Toronto's specific needs. It cites youth unemployment at its highest since 2014, excluding the pandemic years 2020 and 2021, as the reason for the program. The committee referred the item to the Executive Director, Social Development, Finance and Administration for a report back in the fourth quarter of 2025, including an inventory of existing city youth employment programs and the resources needed.

title: Cost-Benefit Analysis of a Pilot for Free Wi-Fi Service on Bus and Streetcar Platforms
topics: Toronto Transit Commission, internet, subway stations, wireless internet; ttc, wi fi; wifi; wireless hotspot
brief: Staff recommended against a pilot for free public Wi-Fi on bus and streetcar platforms, after a cost-benefit analysis found customers prefer faster, no-login cellular service and Wi-Fi use in subway stations fell sharply once 5G arrived. But the TTC Board went beyond staff's advice to forward the findings to the city's ConnectTO program: it directed its chief information officer to partner with the city's chief technology officer on options, innovative solutions and costs for delivering public Wi-Fi across TTC operations, including tunnels, survey customers about their needs, and report back in July 2025 with a final report in October 2025. A station pilot would cost about $59,000 per station to set up and $70,500 per station a year to run; covering all 47 bus and streetcar platforms would cost about $2.8 million upfront and $3.3 million a year to operate.

brief: Commissioner Julie Osborne, seconded by Commissioner Fenton Jagdeo, asks the TTC Board to affirm that prioritizing surface transit is urgent for improving bus and streetcar travel times and reliability. brief: North York Community Council is being asked to direct the General Manager of Transportation to review the history of collisions, deaths and serious injuries on Wilson Avenue between Bathurst Street and Wilson Heights Boulevard and report back on fixes. The motion cites a string of crashes - an 81-year-old woman struck and killed by a dump truck in February 2025, a woman in her 70s struck and killed by a van in January 2025, nine people injured in a TTC bus collision in November 2024, and two more pedestrians hit at Wilson Heights Boulevard in 2023 and 2024 - including better merging of traffic from the 401 off ramps. Pedestrians and motorists on Wilson Avenue would be affected.

title: King High Avenue - Traffic Calming (Speed Humps) and “Watch Your Speed” Signs
topics: driving, traffic, traffic speed; motor vehicle traffic; motorized traffic; traffic conditions; traffic flow; trip info; tripinfo

North York Community Council is asked to authorize speed humps on King High Avenue between Wilson Avenue and Robbie Avenue and a compulsory 3-way stop at King High Avenue and Robbie Avenue, so drivers are aware of their speed through the neighbourhood. Drivers on King High Avenue would be affected.

title: Honouring the Late Michael Mostyn by Naming a Landmark or Site in York Centre
brief: North York Community Council would honour the late Michael Mostyn by naming a landmark or site in York Centre. Mostyn — who earned his law degree at the University of Western Ontario in 1999, joined B'nai Brith Canada in 2006 and rose to CEO in 2014, earned a Queen Elizabeth II Diamond Jubilee Medal in 2012, and helped push provinces and cities to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism — died February 4, 2025 at 50 after a battle with cancer. The naming would recognize his work protecting civil rights and fighting antisemitism.

title: Assigning the Ceremonial Name of “Heroes' Way” to Canterbury Place, North York
brief: Canterbury Place in North York would get the ceremonial name “Heroes' Way”. A ceremonial dedication does not change the official street name or address information; it results in special signage along the street. North York Community Council is asked to assign the name and direct Transportation Services to erect the signage. People on Canterbury Place would see the new signs.

title: 2025 Operating and Capital Budget
brief: The Mayor's proposed 2025 operating and capital budget would go to Council for consideration and approval, as required by the City of Toronto Act. The proposed tax and rate supported operating budget is $18.849 billion gross ($5.639 billion net), and the 2025–2034 capital budget and plan is $59.597 billion gross ($10.524 billion debt), focused on transit ($17.0 billion), transportation ($6.1 billion), and housing ($4.5 billion plus a further $4.5 billion in foregone revenues). The budget began with a $1.2 billion shortfall — a $600 million improvement from the $1.8 billion shortfall in 2024 — and would be balanced with another $680 million in reductions and offsets plus intergovernmental agreements. The budget makes investments in building homes faster, accelerating purpose-built rental approvals and improving services, emergency response times and the City's AA+ credit rating. Every Toronto resident would feel the budget's tax, service and investment decisions.

title: Response to Ontario Regulation 286/09 Budget Matters - Expenses
topics: budgets, capital budgets; budgets and accounts
brief: This is a procedural item about provincial accounting rules. Ontario Regulation 286/09 lets the city leave certain non-cash expenses, such as amortization, out of its balanced cash-basis budget, and the province requires the city to report that exclusion publicly. The report identifies $1.84 billion in excluded expenses and asks council to authorize publishing the information on the city website to satisfy the reporting requirement.

title: Budget Implementation Including Property Tax Rates, User Fees and Related Matters
brief: The 2025 budget now needs the bylaws that make it real. Council is asked to pass the bylaws setting 2025 property tax rates and related user fees, with an average tax-rate increase of 4.37 percent and residential and industrial rates up 5.40 percent. The rates would raise a total 2025 municipal property tax levy of $6.063 billion, including an extra $250.8 million from the 5.4 percent budgetary levy increase and $69.7 million from the City Building Fund levy for priority transit and housing projects. The average Toronto home would pay $4,160 in municipal property tax this year. These rates determine what property owners across Toronto pay this year.

City Council makes the final decision.

title: Designation of the Kensington Market Heritage Conservation District under Part V of the Ontario Heritage Act
topics: heritage conservation districts, heritage preservation; heritage districts; historic areas, historic preservation; historical preservation
brief: Kensington Market would be officially named a Heritage Conservation District, with a plan to guide how the area changes in the future. The plan follows a study started in 2016, prepared with a consultant team and community consultation, and sets place-based policies and guidelines to conserve the area's cultural heritage value. Once designated, new work in the district would have to follow the heritage guidelines. City Council makes the final decision.

title: 1778, 1908, 1914, 1920 and 1926 Bloor Street West - Inclusion on the Heritage Register

Built between about 1927 and 1930, the walk-up apartments were evaluated by staff as having cultural heritage value. Listing recognizes that value but does not ban future changes to the buildings. City Council makes the final decision.

title: 508 and 510 Church Street - Alterations to Heritage Properties and Authority to Amend a Heritage Easement Agreement
topics: heritage designation, heritage preservation, heritage properties; designated heritage properties; heritage buildings; heritage sites; listed heritage properties, historic preservation; historical preservation

Built around 1856-1858 as row houses, these buildings have housed Crews and Tangos — a well-known venue for drag shows and queer gatherings — since 1994, and are a cultural landmark in the Church-Wellesley Village and for Toronto's 2SLGBTQ+ community. The proposal would keep only part of the buildings under a heritage protection agreement.

title: 506-516 Church Street - Official Plan and Zoning By-law Amendment - Decision Report - Refusal

Council would also authorize city lawyers to defend the refusal at the Ontario Land Tribunal.

brief: Thirty-one rental townhouses at 90 Eastdale Avenue and 2 Secord Avenue would be demolished for a 40-storey building with 535 homes, including 35 replacement rentals, under this rental housing demolition application. City Council is asked to approve the change.

The amendment would let the money go toward other purposes such as park improvements, including a splashpad in the ward, at the discretion of the Chief Planner in consultation with the Ward Councillor.
